body: Changelog What arrived, and when. Dates are the day the work landed on the instrument, not the day it was thought of — nothing appears here until it is on the instrument and running. Entries are written for a player: what you can now do that you could not do before. Fixes appear only where they changed what you would see or hear. Unreleased — built and tested, not yet played Everything below this heading is in the repository and passes its tests, and none of it has been through a gate at the instrument. It is here so it is not invisible, and it moves up into a dated entry above once it has been played. Most of this list came out of one session of somebody playing the instrument and saying that something did not sound or look right — which is how every one of these was found, and why none of them had been. A tap you played can no longer be swallowed by the machine writing at the same moment , and a pattern rewrite claims the channel properly rather than assuming it is free. The snapshot tools cannot destroy a snapshot half-way through writing one. Interrupt one now and the file you had is still the file you have. Reverb and delay sends finally mean what they say. A send number is an amplitude now: 100 is unity, 50 is 6 dB down, 25 is 12 dB down, and 30 is a normal, clearly audible send . It used to be a straight line across the plugin’s decibel range, which put 30 at forty-six decibels down — inaudible — and meant you needed three quarters of the knob before a reverb arrived at all. Every effect on the instrument was quieter than its own number claimed. Sends already saved in a snapshot are not rewritten; they now read honestly, so one that had been sitting at an inaudible setting shows as the 0 or 1 it always sounded like. Read SOLO tells you when something is still soloed. Tapping out of solo mode gives the F row back to the mutes and deliberately leaves your solo alone — but nothing said so, and you could walk away from a latched solo with seven channels silent and no lit button anywhere to explain it. SOLO now blinks for as long as anything is soloed, in or out of the mode. Read HOME clears a latched SOLO like every other latch. It was the one modifier the big encoder’s press walked past. Read The first turn after HOME counts. Pressing HOME and turning used to lose that first detent — on the button you reach for precisely when you have stopped knowing where you are. Read MOD’s depth multiplier is on the label. The big encoder under MOD scales every modulator at once and had no readout anywhere, so an out-and-back by hand could leave the whole rig moving less than you meant with nothing to show it. It now reads x0.84 beside the rate whenever it is not 1. Read The MOD pad menu looks inert when it is inert. It is meant to go dim when no modulator is bound — which is the state you are in after loading any snapshot — but “dim” was set bright enough to read as a live menu, so it looked like sixteen working pads that ignored every press. Read Walking the pages quickly is much cheaper. The screens wait for your hand to stop before redrawing, but the wait was short enough that an ordinary, deliberate turn defeated it and repainted both screens on every click. Measured on the instrument: a fast walk through a ring was putting nine hundred messages a second on the link the buttons come back on. The wait is longer now, which costs a fraction of a second before the page you land on appears. LENGTH now says which number it is showing. The word means two things — a drum’s pattern length in beats, a voice’s pitch register in bits — and the column showed the same name and a bare number for both. So turning it on a voice moved a number and changed nothing about how long the pattern was, which reads exactly like a broken encoder. A voice’s column reads LEN BITS now. To make a voice’s loop shorter, turn DIVIDE ; a voice’s pattern is always as long as its division says, and LENGTH sets how many steps the melody takes to repeat — which is its own kind of drift, and a good one. Read HITS says when something is thinning the line. Sixteen hits with a rhythm register masking eleven of them lights five pads, and both numbers were right — nothing said they were different quantities. The column now reads HITS- when fewer steps are sounding than HITS asked for and HITS+ when a tap has added some. The pads still carry how many; this says that the number above them is not the whole story. It matters most when the machine is doing it: a drifting channel keeps thinning under you, and turning HITS back is not the cure people assume. A dead knob says why in the log. A greyed column correctly ignores its encoder — but when one is greyed for a reason you cannot see, “this knob does nothing” was unanswerable without a session at the instrument. REVERB and DELAY now find whatever effect is loaded. (This one is a change to the instrument rather than to a preset, so unlike the rebuilt packs above it is still waiting to be played.) Both encoders used to look their plugin up by name, and only the two factory effects answered — so on a snapshot carrying any other pair both knobs did nothing, both kinds of modulator sat inert, and REVSIZE, REVTYPE, DLYTIME and DLYFBK were dead, with nothing said anywhere. It was true of forty-one of the seventy-one preset snapshots . The verbs resolve by role now. Three limits are real and the surface shows them rather than faking them: REVTYPE’s list of rooms exists on one reverb only, six of the effects are crossfades with no separate dry, and the musical delay division reaches the delays that speak milliseconds. Read A step you erase stays erased. Holding ERASE and tapping a pad took the note straight out of the pattern, while an ordinary tap writes to the register the machine reads when it builds the pattern again — two gestures on the same pads writing to two different places. So on a channel the machine is generating, an erased step came back the moment anything made it rewrite: a turn of HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE, LENGTH or RHYTHM, a reroll, or the channel simply drifting on its own, which needs no hands at all. On a channel you recorded, your notes were always the truth and the erase was always right. Read Three of the twelve modulation rates are gone, and they were never real. Modulation is written a few times a second, so a cycle has to last several times that to come out as a shape. The three fastest — a quarter of a bar, an eighth, a sixteenth — got one or two writes per cycle, which is not a triangle or a ramp but whatever those writes happened to land on, changing bar to bar. They sat on the pad grid fully lit, promising something the instrument could not do. Nothing you have saved moves : the nine that remain are on exactly the pads they were on, and a set saved on one of the three that went comes back on the fastest one left rather than falling silent. Pads 10, 11 and 12 are dark now, and a dark pad that does nothing is the honest version of a lit one that did nothing useful. Read Under the lens, LENGTH says which of the two things it is showing. Spread across all eight channels it was laying pattern beats on the drums beside register bits on the voices — two quantities that cannot be compared, in the one view whose whole job is comparison. The title carries the units now: ALL LENGTH BEATS/BITS . The verb was deliberately not taken away from the lens; the lens replaced five pages that did this, so a verb it refuses is a control you lost. The key stops walking when you have locked every voice. A preset that walks its key was moving it regardless of MOVE, so locking a channel did not lock it against the walker. The limit is worth knowing : the three voices share one key, so locking one of them still cannot hold it — the key moves under it while its neighbours are open. Lock all three and it holds. Read The top line says when it has been cut. It is forty-two characters wide and the panel drops whatever does not fit without a word, and what is appended last is always the newest thing — the bank you are on, a countdown, whether a part is held. An ellipsis at the end marks it now. Switching banks on a channel you had switched to the other kind no longer kills the panel. A channel changed between drum and voice with SHIFT + GRID was rebuilt from the wrong kind when you moved banks, and the panel stopped repainting from that moment — every light and both screens frozen, the bank already changed underneath, the music still playing. That is this instrument's worst failure shape and it took one bank press on a channel a lot of people switch. The set you left behind can no longer play over the set you loaded. Banks you had visited were kept across a snapshot load, so loading one set, visiting bank 3, then loading another and switching to bank 3 gave you the first set's patterns over the second one's sounds. Other banks come back empty now, which is the truth: what a bank holds is not in the snapshot yet. Every encoder stops jumping once a revolution. All eight small encoders were sending one bogus lurch — a big jump one way followed by a big jump back — four times per turn of the knob, because half of each reading was being paired with the other half of the previous one. It has been doing that for as long as the instrument has existed. Slow turns hid it; a sweep did not. A drum step you played keeps its colour across a reload, and a tap no longer takes it off a recording. Played steps show amber so you can see what is yours. On a drum, a played note and a generated one are the same note, so nothing could tell them apart on reload and the amber went — and worse, one pad tap during a session was enough to strip it off a take that was still sounding. The steps are remembered by position now, in the snapshot. Every bank is in the snapshot now, and a set comes back on the bank it was saved on. Banks are scenes — a whole eight-channel arrangement each — and only the one you were playing kept its generator settings; the rest came back with fresh ones. HITS and ROTATE were worse than that : they leaked between banks as you switched, so a rotation set in one bank followed you into the next and was missing from the one you left. Neither can be worked out from the pattern afterwards, so if the instrument does not remember them nothing does. And the sequencer always reloads on bank 1 whatever it was saved on, so a set saved on bank 3 came back as bank 1's patterns underneath bank 3's settings, in silence. A bank you have never visited is still blank, which is the honest answer rather than a gap. Read The screens stopped redrawing whole. Every repaint used to wipe the display and draw it again, so moving one number cost the same as changing everything. The screen is now three separate pieces — the channel tabs, the page line, and each of the four encoder columns — and only the piece that changed is sent. Turning one encoder costs about a seventh of what it did , and selecting a channel about a fifth. This is the last of four goes at the same problem, and it is the one that lets the previous three pay off: the instrument has been able to send just the changed patch of screen since the start of September, and the wipe at the top of every repaint was cancelling it out. Nothing looks different, which is the point — this controller stops answering when it is talked at too fast, and every one of these makes that harder to reach. The web editor and the daemon's own sequencer are gone, and with them a socket anything on your network could reach. The daemon carried a browser page for remapping pads and encoder knobs, served over a connection with no password, by a program running as root — so anything on the same Wi-Fi could change what your pads send and save it to disk. It also carried a complete second sixteen-step sequencer that SHIFT + PAD MODE used to drop you into, taking the pads, PLAY, STOP and the Group buttons away from the instrument with nothing on the panel saying so. Neither had ever been used here; the sequencer this instrument plays is Zynthian's. About eight hundred lines of inherited code removed rather than switched off , and one fewer thing listening on your network. The cost, stated plainly: pad notes and encoder CC numbers are now edited in maschine.json and take a restart, instead of being changeable live in a browser. Read Every encoder stopped lurching four times a revolution — see above; the same round found that the reason written in the code for the guard against it had never been measured. 4 September 2026 — all seventy-one presets rebuilt These are in the instrument, and they went in without an ear gate — deliberately, and it is worth saying which parts of that are checked and which are a judgement. What is checked: every one of the seventy-one crosses a new checker that renders the actual notes and refuses two sustained notes closer together than the ear can separate them at that pitch, two channels on the same note, more things starting at once than the style can carry, a bass that never plays the root of its own key, a mixing board where every fader is identical, and a drone with no layer long enough to sustain. All seventy-one pass. All seventy-one of the version before this one fail. What is a judgement: whether they sound good. Nobody has listened to all of them. The old ones were measurably broken in ways you would have blamed on yourself, so the trade was taken on purpose. All seventy-one preset snapshots were rebuilt, and the drone and ambient ones were the point. They shared one arrangement between twenty files, every channel attacked the same step, and the chord that came out had no root, a minor second at the bottom of it and two voices in exact unison. They were not even drones: on a one-bar grid the longest note the instrument can hold is half a bar, so each one played half a bar of sound, half a bar of silence, and then all eight re-attacked together. They now run four-bar and two-bar layers whose attacks never coincide, hold continuously, and change key on a slow walk. Read Every preset has a mix now. All seventy-one shipped with the eight faders at one identical setting, inherited and never touched — which is not a neutral starting point, it is eight things competing at one loudness. Drums sit forward and voices sit under them, per family. The presets make chords, play grooves you can edit, and swing. None of them made a chord before — chords arrived after the packs were built. Their drum grooves were fixed step lists with nothing behind them, so HITS and ROTATE on the panel showed numbers that had nothing to do with what you were hearing, and the first turn of either wiped the groove; the grooves are euclidean now and the panel agrees with the pattern. Swing and humanisation were zero everywhere and are not. The twenty effect-demo presets became twenty rooms. Eleven of them were note-for-note copies of another preset with a different effect pair, and fourteen could not supply both a reverb and a delay at all. They are now 061 – 080 space , each with its own room, its own key and its own chords. Nineteen different effect pairs, chosen for character. Every preset briefly carried the same two, because that is the only pair where all six effect controls work — and while the knobs looked their plugin up by name it was the only pair that worked at all. Now that they find whatever is loaded, house goes into a small room, deep house into a hall, minimal into the driest plate, dub through a proper dub delay, and the twenty drones each have their own reverb instead of twenty settings of one. Most give up REVTYPE, whose room list exists on the factory reverb alone; on a preset whose reverb already is a particular room, that costs nothing. Read The foundation of a drone cannot drop out. The bottom two layers have their evolution switched off, so only the upper three drift; and a rhythm that evolves its way to silence comes back within a bar or two rather than staying gone. That was checked because there was no listening pass to catch it. 4 September 2026 — the audit’s fixes, played Everything below had been on the instrument since the audit and had never been played. It has now been, across a session at the rig: the panel came up, the pads kept their colours, the chord that used to steal the instrument did nothing and said so in the log, every modifier still meant what it meant, and it was played for a stretch without the daemon dying. The rollback path was run in both directions on purpose, while nothing was wrong. SHIFT + PAD MODE no longer takes the instrument away. That chord stepped the daemon into a sixteen-step sequencer of its own, where the pads stopped sending notes, PLAY and STOP drove the daemon's transport instead of yours, and the Group buttons changed its pages rather than the pad octave. Nothing on the panel said so and it took three more presses of the same chord to get out. The chord is still swallowed, so nothing else about the panel changes; the sequencer behind it is off unless internal_sequencer in maschine.json asks for it. Read The web editor's socket can be closed. It listens on the whole network, has no password, and the daemon runs as root — so anything on your Wi-Fi could remap what the pads send. That is unchanged by default, because closing it would take the editor away from the laptop it is meant to be opened on; what is new is that you can close it in one word, and that the daemon says out loud on every start when it is open. Read The daemon stops dying on things it should shrug off. Sixty places turned an ordinary MIDI-send error into an ended process; a short or garbled report from the controller could crash it or invent a pad hit that nobody played; and its clock arithmetic used the wall clock on a Pi that has no battery for one — so an NTP correction, which on this machine can be days, ended the daemon mid-set. None of that is anything you could see until it happened, and then it was the whole instrument. Rolling a driver back is one command. Every deploy already kept the previous three files; nothing could put them back until now — and now it has been done, on the instrument, and undone again. 3 September 2026 — holding a button stopped redrawing the screens The overlays were the most expensive thing on the panel, and all they change is one line of text. Hold DUPLICATE and the top line names the bank you are on; hold ARM and it counts the bars down; FREEZE puts HELD there, and a channel you have taken over says so. Every one of those redrew both whole screens — once when you pressed, once when you let go. This controller stops answering when it is talked at too fast, and that made a button you hold constantly while playing four times as costly as stepping a page. Now only the line that changed is redrawn. Measured on the instrument: holding DUPLICATE and pressing a Group fell from 308 messages and a peak of 186 a second to 154 and 108 — and what is left is the Group press itself, which really does change what the screens say. The overlay’s own share went from two full screen rewrites to a single row of pixels, and the panel now sends nothing at all to clear a screen when you open one. MOD is deliberately unchanged: it hands every encoder a different job, so the whole screen genuinely does say something new. Nothing looks different anywhere — that is the point. 2 September 2026 — the knobs that lied, and a quieter panel Three knobs took a recorded pattern away without saying so. LEAN, LANE and RHYTHM on a drum each ask the generator for a different pattern, so like HITS and ROTATE they cannot leave a take standing — but where those two hand it back and say so, these three replaced your notes while the channel still called itself yours. They hand back properly now, and the indicator stops reading PLAY the moment they do. Turning one of them down to nothing keeps the take. Read Two knobs on a voice take were pretending to work. RANGE and VELO are only ever read when the generator writes a line, and it does not write a take — so they moved a number on the screen and changed nothing you could hear. They draw ---- now. GATE and OCTAVE stay live, and it is worth knowing why: GATE is the length of a step you tap in, and OCTAVE decides what a pad plays whoever owns the pattern. The big encoder got quieter again. Every page step used to re-park all eight of the small encoders whether or not any had moved. Walking ten pages cost 456 messages to the panel; it costs 192 now, and the busiest moment halved. Nothing about it looks different — that is the point: this controller stops answering when it is talked at too fast, and yesterday’s fix and this one together took the page ring from 674 messages a second to 98. Also: erasing a step removes a whole chord rather than one note of it, and a part that closes through EXIT can no longer be left half-closed if something goes wrong mid-fade. 2 September 2026 — a take can be edited by hand, and a tap no longer eats one A pad tap in STEP mode was deleting recorded patterns. On a channel you own, the tap did not edit the pattern — it told the generator to write the whole thing again, which on a take means the take is gone. The factory snapshot’s hand-played chords on G and H vanished into single notes on the first tap, silently, and the CHORD knob was greyed out at the same time on the grounds that the generator never touches a take. It did. Now the pads edit the pattern, which is what a step grid ought to do. Tap an empty step and a note appears, at the nearest note your take already uses, with your tap’s velocity as its accent; tap a step that sounds and it goes, a chord as a whole chord. Everything else stays exactly where you played it. Read ERASE + a step now removes the whole chord too. It used to remove one note of three and leave the other two sounding while the pad went dark — a step that read as empty and was not. 2 September 2026 — four fixes, and a knob that stopped shouting EXIT works. It has been in the instrument since 1 September and it did nothing: set a channel to 2bar , queue its mute, and it snapped off exactly as if you had never set it. The close was reading the channel’s level from the wrong place — a number the driver keeps that stops matching the fader the moment anything else moves it — so the first instant of a close jumped the strip to that stale value, which sounded like the mute it was supposed to replace. Worse, the landing then wrote that stale number back, so an arrangement gesture quietly rewrote your mix. Both halves are fixed: a close and an open are now a straight ramp over the bars you asked for, and the channel comes back at the level it left from. Read A locked channel says so from every page. MOVE at LOCK stopped the machine touching a channel, and the only place you could see it was the page that set it. Its Group button blinks now, in its own colour — the same blink everything latched on this panel uses. Read The big encoder stopped redrawing the screens for pages nobody read. Walking the page ring cost a full repaint of both displays for every detent your hand passed through, and on this controller that traffic is what makes the panel stop answering — it did, mid-jam. The screens now draw the page you stop on. Measured on the instrument: twenty detents used to cost twenty repaints and a peak of 674 messages a second; they now cost one repaint and a peak of 99. Nothing is lost — a page you walk past is on the glass for about a seventh of a second. Also: the play-session log can see the big encoder at last, which matters only when something goes wrong and then matters a great deal. 2 September 2026 — chords, and a quieter instrument The generator plays chords. CHORD is a new knob on the voice STEP page: seven voicings from a single note up to a five-note ninth, built from scale degrees so every shape stays in the key the three voices share. OFF is note-for-note what the instrument played before, so nothing you already made has changed. It draws dead, and says so, on a channel you have taken over and on a sampler — on the first the generator writes nothing, on the second a note number picks a drum. RANGE moved to the voice’s second AUTO page to make room. That page is now called LINE, because all six of its live knobs answer one question: how the line of pitches is built. CHANCE below 100 breaks a chord into pieces , differently every bar. The sequencer rolls the odds once per note and each chord tone is a note. Deliberate use of it is one of the better things here; it is documented so it is not mistaken for a fault. A long note no longer eats the one after it. With a wide GATE and a busy rhythm, a note reaching the next step that used the same pitch would delete it. It is shortened to fit now instead of vanishing. The instrument stopped redrawing its own screens once a bar. The page indicator carried the bar of the phrase, and a number that changes by itself made the whole display change with it — every bar, for as long as the music ran. On this controller that traffic is the thing that makes the panel stop answering. The count now appears only while something is actually waiting to land, which is the only time it means anything; the countdown was always on the ARM lamp as well. Measured with nobody touching the controller: the display now sends nothing at all between changes. 1 September 2026 — the surface, redesigned Played through at the rig, and the gate found five defects. All five are fixed and in what follows: the light alphabet was unreadable because dim had been chosen on paper and is ten times too bright on real LEDs; the right-hand display froze on a segmented bar given the wrong kind of number; RANGE was a knob that showed a value it could not move; and a kind switch quietly reset the channel’s own play chance, so the screen read 100 while the channel played thinner. The panel was rebuilt around four rules: four modes and a lens, one duration rule for every modifier, one alphabet for every light, and a home to come back to. Four modes instead of five. CONTROL, STEP, AUTO, VOLUME — how it sounds, what it plays, what the machine does by itself, what holds for everything. The generator has a button of its own. Read The lens — hold ALL and the eight encoders become whichever verb your hand last moved, on all eight channels. It replaces every page that existed for one verb. Read HOME — press the big encoder and you are back at STEP, page 1, latches dropped. Nothing armed is lost. Read One duration rule for every modifier — a tap latches, a hold is momentary, so you never have to decide which you meant first. Read Every modifier lights , all saying the same five things: dark, dim, bright, a blink for latched, a pulse for counting down. FREEZE’s two depths are visible for the first time. Read F1–F8 are mutes in every mode , CONTROL included. A plugin switch steps on its own column’s encoder. Read One button regenerates — PATTERN, both kinds, and the selected channel decides which half. A press fires it, a second press before the bar takes it back, and it goes dark when it would do nothing . Read ERASE + SELECT cancels everything armed , now that a tap on SELECT latches the macro pads. Read RANGE reaches the drum CONTROL page — the kit walk’s window has a knob at last. Read 1 September 2026 — the silent-refusal sweep After the gate, every gesture the instrument can decline was checked against what it tells you. The rule it was measured by: a refused gesture that says nothing is the same fault as a channel going quiet without explaining itself. Six were fixed, and three of them were worse than silent — they answered. A drum pad tap adds a hit , not only removes one. The same gesture used to mean two different things on the two kinds: on a voice a tap adds a step, on a drum it did nothing wherever the generator had not already placed one. It was hidden because the tap played the drum either way — a sound that said it had worked. Read A knob that cannot act says so, on every page. Five controls were drawing live on channels that have no such control, and three of them moved a number on screen while changing no sound. Read NOTE REPEAT lights only when it has something to give back. A voice that has never mutated has nothing to undo, and the button now says so instead of sitting lit. Read PATTERN goes dark when a press would do nothing — a reroll refuses on a channel you have recorded onto, and that refusal used to be invisible. Read REC stops promising a take it cannot make while a latched overlay owns the pads. A column with nothing to step through draws dead. A chain with no kits loaded used to show a kit name in normal type with a bar under it, and a knob that did nothing. 1 September 2026 — twelve more things it can do Built and on the instrument the same day. Several were played through during that day’s run at the rig — the AUTO verbs, the bank grid, the phrase page — and the rest are running but have not yet been taken end to end by hand, which is the next thing this project does rather than something the reader has to worry about. New capabilities rather than changes to how the panel works. RULE — a cellular automaton as a second way a register evolves, on both kinds. Read LEAN — a third placement generator beside euclid, weighting hits toward the beat, the eighths or the offbeat. Read LANE — how far the generators may stray, pruning the strays until a bar holds together. Read MOVE — how often the machine may touch a channel at all, as a probability rather than a switch. Read PHRASE and FILL — the fourth bar answers the first. Read EXIT — a part leaves through its filter over a bar or four instead of stopping dead. Read The bank grid — hold DUPLICATE and sixteen pads are sixteen whole arrangements. Read A modulator’s shape, on the screen — a bound column draws a small picture of its wave. Read It says when it has stopped — if generation stops, the indicator says so and the pads keep playing. Read Per-screen brightness and contrast — two settings the daemon applies at start-up. Absent, nothing is read and nothing is written. Half the display traffic — the two screens became independent, so a change on one no longer repaints the other. A style as odds — an offline tool that expresses a snapshot pack as distributions and hard rules, and blends two styles without inventing values for the fields that cannot be averaged. 31 August 2026 — eight features, gated the same day The GEN page for the three voices: ROTATE a melody, MODEL between the shift register and a bounded walk with SPAN and STRIDE, and FEED/AMOUNT so one voice drifts toward another. The drum rhythm register — steps appear and disappear without the line sliding. SWING moved one page along to its spread, where it reaches all eight. A pad tap now flips a bit in the rhythm register on both kinds, so a hand-chosen step survives ROTATE and RHYTHM. HITS, DIVIDE and LENGTH are the way back. The chord walker : the shared root steps along the scale every few bars. The pump — MOD + RESTART snaps every modulator into the same phase. Gate collapse on ARM: every note shortens into the landing and returns. Pad pressure reaches the voices: squeeze a held pad and the filter opens. MIDI export : a tool writes a snapshot’s eight patterns as a standard MIDI file. Seven defects were found during the gate and six fixed the same day — among them ROTATE on a voice, which counted correctly on the display and never changed the sound. 30 August 2026 The surface repaints itself after a replug. Before this, everything but the pads came back dark. The pads stopped sticking, and a slow press sounds. 22 August 2026 A new factory snapshot , with the previous one kept beside it as the way back. A dropped pad light no longer stays wrong forever. 21 August 2026 The factory snapshot ships at 125 BPM , which the sequencer can keep exactly — 124 drifts by a bar every eight minutes. The phrase clock corrects itself against the sequencer, which took its drift from 3,896 parts per million to seven. A held countdown says HELD , and a DROP with nobody nominated refuses out loud instead of muting all eight. A drone and ambient snapshot pack. 20 August 2026 — the performance package The phrase clock and ARM : one bar count for the whole instrument, and gestures that land on a boundary. DROP , BREAK , HALF and DOUBLE , the CHANCE ramp and the ratchet ramp . The mute grid on MUTE, and beat repeat on the transport arrow. The PENDING page , which says what is armed and how long it has left. A master insert — one filter across the whole mix. The moving sweep marker was removed : redrawing it was rebuilding both screens six times a second and taking the controller off the USB bus. What it said — how fast this is moving — became a word on the label instead. 19 August 2026 Drift — the pattern itself moves at the wrap, and refuses on any channel you have taken over. The big encoder became the page ring , so every mode can hold more than one page. RATCHET , REROLL and the kit window. A plugin’s switches reached the F row. HITS and ROTATE were being stored and displayed without reaching the pattern. Fixed at the single write path rather than at the callers. 18 August 2026 The genre pack : fifty ready-made arrangements. A failing wrap was isolated to its own channel, so one bad channel can no longer take the instrument silent. 16 August 2026 The voice generator split in two : MELODY and RHYTHM, so a line’s notes and its rests evolve separately. Played steps on a voice draw amber, so you can see what is yours. Encoder sensitivity halved, with TEMPO held restoring the old speed. 15 August 2026 Navigation buttons stay lit, and the mode buttons go home. REC lights only where recording is possible. 14 August 2026 Modulation : hold MOD and an encoder sets how a value moves rather than what it is. Rates, shapes, depth, and MOD + ERASE to clear. 13 August 2026 — the instrument becomes its own project The driver, the daemon, the installer and the guide moved into one repository, self-contained, with the eight-channel instrument already playing: five euclidean drum channels and three Turing-machine voices. See also Features — the whole instrument in one list What could come next — the idea list, and what was refused

title: Deep parameter control

headings.text: Switches: a knob that steps between words

body: Deep parameter control Eight knobs, and a synth with forty parameters. This is how you reach the fortieth without a menu. What it is Page 1 of CONTROL gives a voice the four controls anyone reaches for first — CUTOFF, RESO, ENV, DECAY. Everything else the plugin publishes fills further CONTROL pages , eight ports to a page, in the plugin's own order and under the plugin's own names. Nothing in the driver knows what those parameters are. It asks the plugin what it has and builds the pages from the answer, which is why a synth nobody planned for still works. On these pages the tab boxes carry the parameter names, not the channel names. A plugin's name rarely fits one row — PitchBend Range and PitchBend Step would both read as PitchBen — so the tab box holds the first line and the row under it holds the second. Sixteen characters, and neighbours stop looking identical. The names are the plugin's own, so a port whose LV2 symbol is output reads Gain . Every other page keeps the channel tabs, which is where a dashed tab still says a channel is not sounding. Try it Select Group G (LEAD) and press CONTROL . That is page 1 — PRESET, CUTOFF, RESO, ENV, DECAY, LEVEL, REVERB, DELAY. Press the right arrow beside the display. Page 2. The names change to the plugin's own — abbreviated to fit, in the order the plugin lists them. Keep pressing. Each page is eight more ports. A large synth runs to several pages. Turn any of them. Each port is driven as a percentage of its own range, so a knob behaves the same whether the port runs 0–1 or 0–20000. Hold TEMPO and turn the same knob. Twice as fast. Hold it to get near, let go to land. Press CONTROL again to jump straight back to page 1 rather than paging around. How it works The four synth knobs follow the plugin that is loaded , not the one the snapshot shipped with. Change a chain's engine from the touchscreen and CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY rebind to the new plugin's own ports. Host plumbing is filtered out. Plugins publish ports no player can use — freewheel flags, latency reports, enable switches that are not really switches. Those are recognised and dropped, so a generated page is eight things you might actually turn. Discreteness is respected. A port with a handful of positions steps in whole units; a continuous one moves by percentage with the remainder carried, so slow turns still move it. A port with named positions steps between those names and never lands between two of them. TEMPO changes how far a turn goes, never what it sets. A speed, not a mode: nothing latches, and the same knob reaches the same values either way. It applies to every encoder on the instrument, not only these. Switches: a knob that steps between words A plugin does not publish one kind of control, it publishes three. Continuous ones are knobs — cutoff, resonance. Switches are not: a filter type is LP24 or BP , an oscillator is saw or square , a section is on or off. A switch column shows the plugin's own word , and the bar under it fills left to right to say where in the list you are — empty or full on a two-position switch. Its own encoder steps it. One position per detent, stopping at each end rather than wrapping, so you can walk the list and arrive where you meant to rather than round it. That is the whole gesture: the column that owns the switch already has a knob under it, so nothing else on the surface has to be spent on this. F1–F8 stay the eight channels' mutes here, as they are in every mode. A row you hit without looking may only mean one thing. Try it Select a synth channel — F, G or H — and press CONTROL . Page right until a column shows a word rather than a four-digit number. Turn the knob below it. The word changes, one position per detent, and stops at each end of the list. What it refuses, and why A one-shot trigger is not offered as a switch. Some plugins publish a port with a single named position — a panic or a re-init. Firing one off a knob you may brush past is not a thing to discover by accident, so those are left alone. A role the plugin has no port for draws dead. If a loaded synth publishes no resonance, the RESO column greys out and its encoder does nothing at all. That is the same law the whole surface follows: a knob with no source is drawn dead rather than showing a number it cannot move. A knob that silently does nothing is the worst object on a control surface, because you cannot tell it apart from a broken one. See also Sound and presets — page 1, and changing the engine underneath it Modulation — every generated port can carry a modulator

title: Every feature, and where it is written up

headings.text: The surface, and keeping what you made

body: Every feature, and where it is written up This is the whole instrument in one list. Each row says what a feature does in a sentence and links to the page that walks you through it on the real hardware. It exists because the guide is organised by what you are doing — generating, playing, mixing, saving — which is the right shape for learning and the wrong shape for the question “does it do X?”. This page answers that question and nothing else. If something you expected is missing, it may be deliberate: What could come next carries the idea list and, at the end of it, what was considered and refused , with the reason. Generating patterns The generator owns the pattern. You set the odds and the shape; it writes the notes into the sequencer at every wrap. Feature What it does Where Euclidean drums Five drum channels, always alive. HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE and LENGTH; the generator writes the notes. Generating patterns Per-step odds Hold SHIFT and tap a pad to ladder that one step through 100, 75, 50 and 25 per cent. A step that sounds sometimes SWING, VELO, OCTAVE and RANGE The four knobs that shape what the generator writes rather than deciding it. SWING is per channel. SWING, VELO, OCTAVE and RANGE CHORD The generator plays more than one note at a time. Seven voicings built from scale degrees, so every shape stays in the key. Draws dead on a take and on a sampler. CHORD Six scales MIN, MAJ, DOR, PHR, HMIN and PENT, shared by all three voices. The chord walker Turing-machine voices Three voices, each evolving its own shift register into a melody. How it works A pattern rebuilt every cycle The bar is regenerated rather than looped, so it does not come back around identical. How it works Polymeter LENGTH reaches three, five and seven beats against a four-to-the-floor kick. Lengths that do not agree Probability per channel CHANCE, read live while the pattern plays, so a step sounds only sometimes. A step that sounds sometimes Ratchets RATCHET fires one step several times inside its own slot. RATCHET Reroll One button asks for a different bar from the same settings; the selected channel decides which half of the instrument it touches, and a second press before the wrap takes it back. Reroll The drum rhythm register Steps appear and disappear bar to bar without the line sliding sideways. A pad tap goes into the same register — taking a hit out or putting one in — and survives ROTATE. The drum rhythm register A wandering voice MODEL switches a voice between its shift register and a bounded walk, with SPAN and STRIDE. The voice AUTO page Voices that listen to each other FEED and AMOUNT drift one voice’s register toward another’s — related, never identical. The voice AUTO page ROTATE on a melody The whole line turns around the bar, notes and rests together. The voice AUTO page A cellular automaton RULE evolves a register by looking at each step’s neighbours instead of rolling dice, so shapes travel and collide. RULE A generator that leans LEAN weights hit positions by what the part is for — the floor, the eighths, or the offbeat. LEAN A constraint on the generators LANE measures a bar and removes the hits furthest from the beat until it holds together. LANE Per-channel automation depth MOVE is how often the machine may touch a channel at all. At LOCK it holds while everything else moves — and its Group button blinks, so you can see the lock from any page. MOVE A phrase with a fill PHRASE and FILL make every second or fourth bar answer the ones before it. PHRASE and FILL Key and scale, shared ROOT and SCALE are global and land on the bar, so three voices cannot drift out of key. The chord walker A chord walker The shared root steps along the scale every few bars, reflecting at the edge of its span. The chord walker Playing and recording Feature What it does Where The pads play Sixteen pads, the selected channel’s sound, over whatever the generator is doing. title: Generating patterns

RATCHET — a step that fires more than once

body: Generating patterns You do not draw a beat. You set hits, rotation and randomness, and the generator writes the notes. This is the machine's centre — everything else colours what happens here. What it is The driver writes real notes into Zynthian's own sequencer . Not a private buffer: because they are real notes in the real sequencer, patterns persist in snapshots and the touchscreen pattern editor mirrors exactly what the pads show. There are two generators, and every channel runs one of them: Euclidean , on the five drum channels. Given a step count and a hit count, hits spread as evenly as the grid allows, then rotate. Two Turing machines , on each of the three voices. One shift register is read as pitch, the other as which steps sound. Each is clocked once per pass and mutated by its own knob — MELODY and RHYTHM — so a melody can evolve over a rhythm that stays exactly where you put it. Which generator a channel runs is not fixed to its engine — see Sound and presets . Try it The drums. Press Play , then Group A to select KICK, then STEP . Turn encoder 1 (HITS) to 4. That is four-on-the-floor. Turn encoder 2 (ROTATE). The same four hits slide around the bar without changing how many there are. Turn HITS to 5. Five in sixteen is the clave. Try 3 in 8 for tresillo, or 7 in 16 for the busy one that still swings. The voices. Press Group F for BASS, then AUTO — a voice’s generators live there. Turn encoder 3 (MELODY) to about 30. The bassline starts fishing: every pass mutates one bit, so the line keeps turning into a neighbouring line. When a phrase goes past that you want, snap MELODY back to 0. The cell reads LOCK and that line is frozen, bit for bit, until you move the knob again. Missed it? Press NOTE REPEAT . It gives the previous line back and sets both knobs to 0 so it holds. Now put MELODY at LOCK and turn encoder 4 (RHYTHM) to about 30. The opposite: the notes hold still while steps appear and disappear underneath them. Both at LOCK, then press STEP and tap pads. Each tap turns a step on or off, and it stays — tap step 1 and step 9, then turn MELODY up, and you have two notes evolving on the beat you chose. A KICK B SNAR C CLAP D CHAT HITS 0004 ROTATE 0000 DIVIDE 1/16 LENGTH 0016 The drum STEP page. HITS and ROTATE are the two you play with; DIVIDE and LENGTH set the frame. How it works The drum STEP page is HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE, LENGTH, VELO, CHANCE, RATCH, SWING. HITS and ROTATE are the two you play with; the rest set the frame. CHANCE is how often a hit actually fires — drop it and the pattern starts breathing rather than repeating. The voice STEP page is DIVIDE, LENGTH, GATE, OCTAVE, CHORD, VELO, CHANCE, SWING. LENGTH here is the pitch register’s length in bits, not a bar count — and the column says so: it reads LEN BITS on a voice and plain LENGTH on a drum. GATE is how long each note holds — up to eight steps, so a pad can be a drone. The pitch value is quantised to ROOT and SCALE from VOLUME’s GLOBAL page, then placed by OCTAVE and RANGE — RANGE lives one page over, on LINE. The two generators are not on STEP. They are on AUTO. STEP is what a channel plays; AUTO is what the machine does to it by itself, and MELODY and RHYTHM are the second question rather than the first. A drum’s RHYTHM is there for the same reason: it is the machine making up the part, not you setting the frame it is made in. One verb across all eight is a hold, not a page. Put your hand on CHANCE or SWING, hold ALL , and the eight encoders become that one verb on every channel at once — the page indicator reads ALL CHANCE so you know which one you are looking at. It is the fastest way to swing or thin the whole kit without walking the channels one at a time, and the fastest way to see why one channel is not behaving like the other seven. MELODY is the instrument’s main gesture. Set it to 20–40 and the voice fishes. Snap it to 0 the moment you hear something worth keeping. The cell reads LOCK rather than a number, deliberately: a number could be a coincidence, while LOCK means nothing will rewrite that pattern at all. Both ends of MELODY are periodic, and only the middle is unpredictable. This surprises everyone once, so it is worth knowing before it happens to you: MELODY What you get LOCK (0) the same bar, bit for bit, forever 20–40 the line fishes — a neighbouring line each pass. This is the useful range around 50 the most unpredictable it gets 100 a two-bar loop. Not chaos At 100 every fed-back bit is flipped rather than sometimes flipped, so one pass gives you the exact inverse of the register and the next gives you the original back — pattern, inverse, pattern, inverse. It sounds like the generator has stopped evolving, and in a sense it has: it is evolving into a cycle of two. If you want it to keep surprising you, keep it below about 60. The same is true of RHYTHM, for the same reason. RHYTHM is the same gesture applied to the beat. Same range, same LOCK at zero, same freeze. Which steps sound is its own register, one bit per step, so it is independent of the notes: either can run while the other holds. A pad tap in STEP mode flips one of those bits, which is why a rhythm you tap in by hand survives everything — it is not an edit sitting on top of the generator, it is the generator. Structure lands on the bar; timbre lands instantly. A change to what the pattern is waits for the channel's own next wrap, so the groove never jumps under your hand. DIVIDE and LENGTH show in angle brackets — >1/8< — while a change is waiting to take. What it refuses, and why Pattern length is quantised to whole beats, and always will be. The sequencer stores a pattern as a number of beats, so the reachable step counts are whole beats times the steps in a beat. Turning LENGTH lands on the nearest count that exists rather than refusing to move — so if the number skips past where you aimed, that is the grid and not a fault. Which step counts you can reach depends on DIVIDE, not on the sequencer. At 1/16 a beat is four steps, so LENGTH moves in fours: 4, 8, 12, 16. At 1/4 a beat is one step, so every count from 1 to 16 is available. An odd number that DIVIDE cannot express is not missing from the instrument — it is on another division. A silent channel says so. HITS at 0 is a silent channel, not a broken one, and CHANCE at 0 emits nothing at all. Both draw the channel's tab dashed — the instrument's one mechanism for explaining silence. Read the tab row before suspecting the rig. Lengths that do not agree A voice’s loop length comes from DIVIDE, not LENGTH A voice’s pattern is always exactly as long as its division says , because the generator restamps it on every rewrite. So the reachable loops are half a bar, one, two or four — plus the two triplet grids, which are twelve steps rather than sixteen. Turning LENGTH on a voice will never shorten it. That is not the loss it sounds like, because LENGTH is already a drift control. The register repeats every LENGTH steps while the rhythm repeats every sixteen, so the melody walks against its own pattern: LENGTH 5 comes home every five bars, LENGTH 3 every three. That is the whole idea of a Turing machine and it is what the knob has always done. For a loop of a genuinely odd length — seven steps against sixteen — use a drum channel at DIVIDE 1/4. There a beat is a step, so LENGTH 7 is seven steps, and it meets a sixteen-step channel again after seven bars. Drum lengths are free; only voices are pinned to their division. LENGTH is per channel, and nothing makes the eight agree. Give the kick four beats and the hat three, and they start together, drift apart, and meet again twelve beats later. Nothing is generating that — it is two loops of different lengths running side by side, which is the oldest trick in machine music and costs one encoder turn here. Set it on the STEP page with LENGTH . Every other channel is untouched, because length was never global. Which lengths each division reaches A pattern has to fit the sixteen pads, so the finer the division, the fewer beats it holds: DIVIDE Beats you can set Steps that gives 1/32 1–2 8, 16 1/16 1–4 4, 8, 12, 16 1/8 1–8 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 1/16T 1–2 6, 12 1/8T 1–5 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 1/4 1–16 every count from 1 to 16 Odd beat counts live at 1/8, 1/8T and 1/4. Three, five and seven beats are all reachable there. At 1/16 and finer they are not — a five-beat pattern at 1/16 would be twenty steps and there are sixteen pads to show it on. Try it Leave the kick on group A at four beats. Put a hat on group B, set DIVIDE to 1/8 and turn LENGTH down to three beats. Let it run: the hat walks around the kick and lands back on the one every twelve beats. Take group C to five beats and the three of them do not agree again for sixty. Shortening keeps the steps that fit and drops the ones past the new end; growing back leaves the new steps empty rather than restoring what a shrink discarded. A step that sounds sometimes Hold SHIFT and tap a step to set how often it plays. Each press steps it down — always, three times in four, half the time, one time in four — and the fifth press brings it back to always. A bare tap still turns the step on and off; SHIFT is what changes the odds. While SHIFT is held the pads show the odds instead of the pattern. Each step takes its own colour, brightest magenta for always, then red, then orange, and a cool pale blue for the rarest — so the one that hardly ever fires is obvious without comparing it to its neighbours. Let go and the step picture comes back. The white playhead keeps sweeping over the top either way. This is the gentlest way to make a bar stop repeating itself. A hat at three-quarters and a clap at half will not play the same bar twice, but the pattern you wrote is still the pattern — nothing is being regenerated behind your back. It is safe on a take you have recorded. Setting the odds does not rewrite the pattern: no step is moved, added or removed, so unlike turning HITS or ROTATE it cannot hand your take back to the generator. It costs nothing to try mid-jam, and the odds are saved in the snapshot with everything else. RATCHET — a step that fires more than once RATCHET is encoder 7 on a drum's STEP page. Turn it up and every step of that channel fires two, three or four times inside its own slot — a roll rather than a hit. It reads OFF at the bottom, because one hit is not a ratchet. It applies to the whole channel, not one step, which is what makes it a knob rather than an edit: turn it up for a bar of rolls and back down again without touching the pattern you wrote. SWING, VELO, OCTAVE and RANGE — the four that shape rather than generate Four encoders on the STEP pages do not decide which steps exist. They decide how the steps that do exist come out, and they are the ones a reader most often walks past. Knob Where What it does SWING encoder 8, both STEP pages How far the offbeats are pushed late, from 50 to 75 . 50 is dead straight and the machine's default; the mid–fifties are where a straight techno bar starts to walk; the top is a hard shuffle. It is per channel , which is the point — a swung hat over a straight kick is most of what makes a groove feel played. Put the lens on it to set all eight at once. VELO encoder 5 (drum), 6 (voice) How hard every generated step is struck, 1 to 127. Under a velocity–layered kit this is a timbre knob as much as a level one: turn it down and a sampled snare finds its quieter layer rather than just getting smaller. It sets what the generator writes; a step you played in by hand keeps the velocity your finger gave it. OCTAVE encoder 4, voice STEP Moves the whole voice up or down, −2 to +2 octaves, without touching a note it chose. This is how three voices sharing one key and one scale stop crowding each other — BASS down, PADS up, and the same walker suddenly sounds arranged. RANGE encoder 6, voice AUTO page 2 (LINE) How many octaves the register is allowed to spread its notes over. Small and the line stays put and sounds like a riff; wide and it leaps and sounds like a machine. OCTAVE moves the window, RANGE sizes it. It spreads upward from the root , not symmetrically around it, so widening RANGE lifts the line as well as opening it out. On a euclidean drum, OCTAVE and RANGE draw dead . A sampled kit has no register to spread and no octave to move it in, and a knob that turned a number without changing a sound is exactly the lie this surface refuses. The CHANCE ramp — the kit thins out and re-forms Hold ARM — that is SELECT — tap pad 2, then tap a length. The gesture is on The surface ; this is what it does. From the landing bar every channel's play chance walks down, one step per bar. Halfway through the length all eight are at one time in four — still playing, but most of it missing — and over the second half they walk back up. An eight-bar ramp is four bars falling apart and four bars coming back. It lands back on each channel's own value, not on always. A channel sitting at half the time comes back at half the time. Assuming everything wants to be at full is exactly how a channel saved quiet comes back loud, and this does not do it. A channel already at one time in four or below is left alone. A breakdown that made a quiet channel louder would be the gesture backwards. It is safe on a take you recorded. Play chance belongs to the pattern rather than to the notes: nothing is regenerated, no step is moved, added or removed, and the ramp writes once per bar rather than continuously. Same reason SHIFT + pad is safe. Play chance is in the snapshot, so a set saved mid-ramp saves the thinned values. Let it finish before you save. HALF and DOUBLE — the same rhythm, at another speed Arm HALF or DOUBLE and every generated channel changes speed on the bar, then changes back. The pattern is not redrawn coarser or finer: the step count is kept and the beat count moves with the division, so what you hear is the rhythm you already had, played at half or twice the speed. Some channels cannot make the move, and the display says how many did. HALF 5/8 means five of the eight went. A division needs somewhere to go: 1/8 triplet has no half-speed partner, 1/4 has none either, and 1/32 and 1/16 triplet cannot double. Double-time also needs an even number of beats to halve. A channel that cannot move is left exactly as it was rather than approximated. Straight stays straight and triplet stays triplet. A speed change that turned a straight channel into a triplet one would be a second, unasked-for change riding along with the first. It comes back to what was captured , not to a calculated opposite — drift, reroll and the encoders can all move a channel while the macro is out, and only the snapshot taken at the moment it fired is reliable. Channels you have recorded onto are left alone. The move regenerates from the generator settings, and a take has none to regenerate from. Under polymeter it can arrive up to a bar late on the odd channels. The macro fires on the phrase bar, but a structure change is taken at each channel’s own wrap — the same rule that stops a division change tripping the groove mid-bar. On a rig where every channel is four beats the question never comes up. The ratchet ramp — the roll into the drop Arm the ratchet ramp and every drum note subdivides further each bar , arriving at x4 exactly on the last bar of the length you chose. A four-bar arm walks 1–2–3–4; a two-bar arm goes 1 then 4. It always arrives — a build that stopped at x3 because you armed three bars would be a build that never lands. Each channel goes back to its own RATCHET setting afterwards, so a channel you had already left ratcheting comes back ratcheting. Voices are skipped, and so are recorded channels. RATCHET is a drum verb — it is written into the notes as sequencer stutter, and a voice’s pattern comes from a different generator entirely, so taking the voices too simply overwrote their melodies. Recorded channels are left out for the same reason as everywhere else: the ramp rewrites the pattern from the generator settings each bar. The page indicator says how many channels it took — ROLL 3/8 means three of the eight are rolling and five are not. Three drums and five voices is a normal reading, not a fault; so is a lower number when you have recorded onto a drum. Reroll — one button that asks for a different bar Press PATTERN to reroll the channel you are on. A drum channel gets a new hit count and rotation; a channel played by the Turing register gets a new rhythm and a new play chance, and its MELODY is left at LOCK so you hear the new line held rather than already drifting. Hold SHIFT to reroll a whole family at once — every channel of the same kind as the one you have selected. On a drum that is every sampler; on a voice, every synth. The split follows the engine rather than how a channel is being played, so a drum sampler switched to Turing is still a sampler, and asking for new synth lines never hands you a new drum pattern as well. To reroll all the drums while looking at a voice, select a drum first. The button goes dark when a press would do nothing. A reroll refuses on a channel you have recorded onto — it would throw your take away — and a refusal you cannot see is the same fault as a channel going quiet without saying why. Hold SHIFT and it lights again, because the wider scope has other channels to work on. It lands on the bar, and the wait is the point. The press arms it: the display reads REROLL> straight away and the tabs of the channels it will hit are drawn dotted , so you see what is about to change before it does. Press the same button again before it lands and it is cancelled. It never touches a channel you have recorded on. Those channels are simply left out, and their tabs stay undotted — the drums have no undo, so a reroll that included them would be a data-loss button. If you want a recorded channel rerolled, hand it back first with ERASE + Group. It cannot leave a channel silent. A drum always keeps at least one hit, a voice always keeps some steps and a play chance above a floor. Silence with nothing to explain it is the one thing this instrument refuses to produce, and a reroll that muted a channel by accident would be exactly that. ERASE and the same button puts it back — one deep. ERASE is the take-it-back gesture everywhere on this instrument, and SHIFT is spoken for here. The voice AUTO page — how a voice invents its line Press AUTO on a voice and you get everything the machine does to it without being asked: the two generators, and the controls that change how it makes up a melody rather than what that melody currently is. Page on once and you reach WALK , which holds the line rotation and the walk’s own settings. ROTATE , on the WALK page, turns the whole line around the bar, the way it always has on the drums. The notes keep their order and their shape; they simply start somewhere else. Like every other parameter knob it stops at each end rather than wrapping round — only the big encoder cycles. MODEL , on the AUTO page beside MELODY, chooses which generator the voice uses. Turn it right for a wandering voice and left for the shift register it has always had. The register flips bits at random, so its line jumps about; the walk moves by steps, so its line strolls. They sound like different instruments rather than different settings. SPAN is how far the walk may stray from where it started, and STRIDE is how big each step is; both are on the WALK page, and both draw dead until MODEL is on the walk, because until then there is no walk for them to shape. FEED and AMT , also on the WALK page, make one voice listen to another. Point FEED at a different voice and raise AMOUNT, and this voice’s register drifts toward that one’s over the following bars — related, never identical. It is a slow effect and it only acts at the bar. Two things to know: it rides the register’s own mutation, so MELODY has to be off LOCK or nothing happens at all ; and a voice cannot be fed to itself. The wheel steps over its own channel, because a control that appears to do nothing is worse than one that refuses. All of them are held by FREEZE and refused on a channel you have taken over by playing it, exactly like everything else that rewrites a pattern. The drum rhythm register — the soft randomiser The voices have always had a generator that evolves. The drums have the same one. On a drum’s AUTO page, encoder 3 is RHYTHM , and turning it up lets steps appear and disappear from bar to bar instead of the euclid line repeating exactly. Watch what it does and does not do: steps come and go, and the pattern never slides sideways . Sliding is rotation, that is a separate control, and this one must not quietly consume it. At zero it reads LOCK , the same word MELODY uses, and holds the line still. Tapping a step goes into the same register. Tap a lit pad and that hit stops sounding; tap it again and it comes back. Tap a dark pad and you get a hit there — one the generator never placed. What you tapped is part of what the generator knows, not an edit sitting on top of it, so it survives ROTATE and RHYTHM and is saved with the snapshot for nothing. Turning the line round carries your edits with it: you took out, or put in, a hit rather than a position on the grid, and it stays wherever the line is turned to. The pad makes a sound only when the tap adds something. Putting a hit in plays it so you hear what you just placed; taking one out is silent, because the pad going dark has already told you and playing a step you just removed would say the opposite. HITS, DIVIDE and LENGTH are the start-again knobs. Move any of them and every step goes back into the register, so the plain euclid line returns. That is the way back — without it, a pattern you had tapped holes in could only be restored by tapping every hole shut again. The three of them go together because they all decide how many steps exist, and a hole in step 15 means something else the moment the pattern is twelve steps long. HITS stops being the number of hits you hear, and that is the trade. It is what the generator draws; what you hear is that, minus what you tapped out, plus what you tapped in. Every generator control here works that way already — MELODY does not tell you how many notes a voice plays either — and the pads are the truth about what sounds. A tap is always honoured, including on a channel you have taken over by playing it. The generator still stands off such a channel — that is what taking it over means — but your own hand is not refused on the grounds that your hand was there first. CHORD — the generator plays more than one note at a time A voice has always played one note per step. CHORD , on the voice STEP page, stacks notes on top of that one — the line it was already playing keeps its shape and its root, and gains a voicing. Seven settings: OFF , OCT the same note an octave up, 5TH root and fifth, TRI a full triad, SUS the third replaced by a fourth, 7TH the flat seventh on top, and 9TH , five notes and the widest it goes. OFF sounds exactly like the instrument did before chords existed , note for note, so nothing you already made has changed. They are stacks of scale degrees, not semitones. The three voices share ROOT and SCALE, so a chord built from fixed intervals would walk straight out of the key you set; built from degrees, every shape stays diatonic and a triad on one degree comes out minor while the same setting on another comes out major. That is the scale doing its job, not the knob being inconsistent. An octave is however many degrees the scale has, which is seven in five of the six scales and five in PENT — so OCT is still an octave in pentatonic, and the wider shapes are correspondingly tighter. CHORD draws dead on two kinds of channel, and says so. On a channel you have taken over by playing it, the generator does not write the pattern at all, so a chord setting would move a number and change no sound. On a sampler, a note number picks a drum rather than a pitch, so a stack of degrees would add unrelated hits. In both cases the column is grey, reads ---- , and the knob does nothing — which is the surface telling you the truth rather than pretending. CHANCE below 100 breaks a chord into pieces, and you may want that. The sequencer rolls the odds once per note , and every tone of a chord is its own note, so a triad at 70 becomes a different subset of itself bar by bar — a stab that flickers between two and three voices. It is not a setting anyone chose; it falls out of how the sequencer works and it cannot be turned off from here. Used deliberately it is one of the better things on the instrument; used by accident it sounds like the chords are broken. Measured on the rig: with CHORD off, the bass channel sent one note per step. With TRI, exactly three times as many notes in the same window, the root of every chord unchanged, and all four chords diatonic. The chord walker — three voices, one progression This is not CHORD, and the names are close enough to be worth separating. CHORD stacks notes at one moment. The walker moves the key underneath everything over bars — a progression rather than a voicing. They are good together and they are different controls. ROOT and SCALE are shared: all three voices pick their notes from the same key, and a key change lands on the bar. The walker moves that root for you. SCALE has six positions , and they are the six a techno record actually uses: MIN natural minor, MAJ major, DOR dorian, PHR phrygian, HMIN harmonic minor and PENT minor pentatonic. They run roughly from most familiar to most opinionated — DOR is minor with a lift in it, PHR is the flat second that makes a bassline sound menacing, HMIN is the one that will sound like a soundtrack if you leave it on, and PENT has no semitones at all, so nothing a voice invents inside it can clash. If a generated line sounds wrong rather than surprising, PENT is the place to go and find out whether it is the notes or the rhythm. Press VOLUME for the GLOBAL page. WALK is how often the root moves, in bars, and SPAN is how far it may wander. At zero WALK reads LOCK and the key stands still. Every WALK bars the root steps to a new degree of the scale you are already in — never chromatically, because three voices sharing a scale should not be walked out of it. It reflects at the edge of its span rather than parking against it, and a walk that returns to zero returns to exactly the key you dialled in, not near it. Measured on the instrument: at four bars and 121 BPM the root moved every 7.9 seconds, which is four bars to within a twentieth of a second, and every root it visited belonged to the same minor key. RULE — a second way a register evolves Everything that evolves on this instrument has done it the same way: a bit flips at random, and MELODY or RHYTHM is how often. RULE offers the other kind of change. Instead of rolling dice per step, it looks at each step’s neighbours and applies a rule — so a shape can travel along the bar, collide with another, and come out the far side. One sentence for the difference: RAND reshuffles, the R-rules move things. Under RAND a hit can vanish here and appear anywhere; under a rule it steps to the next position, grows a neighbour, and dies where two of them meet. To hear which you have, make the pattern sparse — three hits, RHYTHM around the middle — and watch the pads for a few bars. With sixteen hits every rule looks like noise. It is encoder 1 of the AUTO page, on both kinds. Four settings, and the first is what you already have. RAND — the shift register, unchanged. This is where every channel starts. R30 — scatters. Busy and rarely repeating. R90 — diagonals. Shapes drift across the bar and cancel where they meet. R110 — the interesting one. Structures form, survive for bars, and are disturbed by whatever passes. MELODY and RHYTHM still mean the same thing. On the shift register they are how likely the fed-back bit is to flip; on a rule they are how likely the rule is to be applied to each step, with the rest held. So LOCK is still exactly LOCK on either, and a channel at the top of the knob is the pure automaton. These rules are deterministic: the same bar leads to the same next bar. That is what makes a shape survive long enough to be heard rather than dissolving into noise. One consequence is worth knowing — if the pattern ever empties completely, a single step is put back . Every rule of this kind maps an empty bar to an empty bar, so without that the channel would go silent for good with the knob still reading a number. LEAN — a generator that leans Euclid spaces hits evenly. That is its virtue and its limit: it cannot write a hat line that leans on the eighths, or a percussion part that lives on the offbeat, because it has no opinion about where the beat is. LEAN is a second placement generator, on encoder 2 of the drum AUTO page. It weighs the positions by what the part is for . EUCL — euclid, exactly as before. Every existing channel is here. BEAT — the floor. Hits land on the quarters, and extras flam just after them. 8TH — hats. The eighths first, then the sixteenths between. OFFB — syncopation. The “and” of each beat, and the downbeat last of all. Ask for more hits than the grid has room for and they spread : eight on BEAT is a flam on each beat, not four hits crowded onto beat one. The late one comes before the early one, because that is what these parts do. ROTATE still rotates a leaning channel , and that is deliberate. Turning the line moves its accents off the grid they were built against, which is a real musical consequence — but the alternative was to make ROTATE do nothing here, and a knob that quietly does nothing is the worst thing this surface could offer. The pads show you where the hits went. LANE — how far the generators may stray LANE is encoder 4 of the drum AUTO page. One number per drum channel: how narrow the danceable lane is. At RAW you get the raw field — whatever the generators wrote, which is what the instrument has always played. Turn it up and each bar is measured before it is allowed out: the hits furthest from the beat are removed until what is left holds together. At the top only what lands on the beat survives. It replaces fiddling with six controls at once when a channel gets away from you. It only ever removes — it will not invent a hit, so HITS goes on meaning the number of hits the generator was asked for — and it will never empty a channel : the last hit survives whatever the knob says. The three voices have no LANE at all — hold ALL with your hand on it and their three columns draw dead. That is not an oversight. A voice’s placement is its rhythm register, and a tap on a voice pad writes into that same register — so a lane on a voice would quietly undo steps you put in by hand. MOVE — how much the machine may move a channel MOVE is encoder 5 of the AUTO page, on both kinds. One number per channel, and it answers the question LANE does not: not how far the machine may go, but how often it may touch this channel at all. At LOCK the channel holds its pattern bar to bar and every automatic gesture leaves it alone — the tops can move while the kick stays exactly where you put it. At 100, which is where every channel starts, everything behaves as it always has. In between it is a probability , not a switch. At 50 the machine touches the channel about half the time it would have, which is a different instrument from a channel that is simply frozen: it still surprises you, just less often. If you want the hard version, FREEZE is the button for it. It gates the bar-rate gestures too — the ratchet and chance ramps, HALF and DOUBLE, the drop. Those used to walk every channel whether or not you had an opinion about that one. A locked channel says so from every page. Its Group button blinks, in its own colour, once a second — the same blink every latched thing on this panel uses, because that is what LOCK is: a decision you made and walked away from. It stops the moment MOVE leaves 0. A muted channel stays dark instead: dark on that row means “not sounding”, and the machine being kept off something you cannot hear is not the thing you need told. PHRASE and FILL — the fourth bar answers the first Encoders 6 and 7 of the AUTO page. PHRASE is how long a channel’s phrase is — BAR , 2bar , 3bar or 4bar , and the odd one is there on purpose: a channel on 3bar against the rest on 4bar takes twelve bars to come back round — and FILL is how full its last bar gets. Set a channel to 4bar and raise its FILL, and every fourth bar comes back busier before the plain pattern returns. The added steps go to the offbeats first, because a fill that added hits on the beats would just be a louder version of the bar it is supposed to answer. A fill only ever adds. Taking hits away is a breakdown, and there are knobs for that. At BAR and OFF , which is where everything starts, no bar is ever a fill.
