title: Mixing and effects

headings.text: DROP — everything falls away but the ones you kept
BREAK — fall out now, come back on the bar
The master insert — one filter across the whole mix
The effects this is proven on
The knobs find the effect, whatever it is
Five that are out, and why
EXIT — a part that leaves rather than stops

body: Mixing and effects Balancing eight channels from eight knobs, the two effects every channel feeds, and the handful of settings that belong to the machine rather than to a channel. What it is Every channel carries its own reverb and delay send on encoders 7 and 8, feeding two shared effects. Sixteen insert hosts in total — a TAP Stereo Echo and a TAP Reverberator on every one of the eight channels. The sends are post-fader , so pulling a channel down takes its tail with it rather than leaving a ghost of it hanging in the reverb. A send number is an amplitude, and it behaves the way a mixer would lead you to expect. 100 is unity — the wet as loud as the signal feeding it. Halving the number takes off 6 dB, so 50 is −6, 25 is −12, and 10 is −20. 30 is a normal, clearly audible send , which is where most of these want to sit. 0 is off. There is no boost at the top: 100 is unity and the knob stops there. A wet return louder than its own source is not something you should be able to ask for by turning a knob to the end. Try it Press CONTROL. Encoders 6, 7 and 8 are LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY on every channel, whatever it plays. Hold ALL and turn encoder 6. The row becomes eight LEVELs, one per channel, and the page indicator reads ALL LEVEL . That is the page for balancing, and it is a hold rather than a place. Let go, put your hand on encoder 7, then hold ALL again. Now it is eight REVERB sends. Encoder 8 gives you eight DELAYs the same way. Tap ALL instead of holding it and the lens latches. Tap it again to drop it. Move CUTOFF on a voice and hold ALL. Three columns answer and five draw dead — the drums have no filter to reach. See below. Press VOLUME. Now the eight encoders are the machine's globals: ROOT, SCALE, BPM, WALK, SPAN, MASTER, REVSIZE, DLYTIME. How it works A page is eight verbs on one channel. The lens is one verb on eight channels. That is the whole grammar of the surface, and it is why there are no mixer pages to go looking for: hold ALL and whichever verb your hand last moved lays itself out across the eight channels, then let go and you are back where you were. Every channel verb can be looked at that way — the sends, the filter, swing, play chance, how much rope a channel is given — without the instrument growing a page for each. A channel that does not carry that verb draws dead , in the usual way: ---- , a lower-case name and no bar. So CUTOFF across the eight is three live columns and five dead ones, and LANE is the other way round. Turning a global — BPM, ROOT, MASTER — or a name like KIT or PRESET does not move the lens, because there is nothing to lay side by side; it stays on whatever it last held, and before you have moved anything at all it shows LEVEL. ROOT and SCALE wait for the bar , like everything else that changes what the pattern is. The rest of the globals land instantly. Group button brightness tracks each channel's level , so the row shows the balance without reading anything — and the peak meters on the display run live. DROP — everything falls away but the ones you kept Hold ARM — that is SELECT — tap pad 1, then tap a length. The gesture itself is on The surface ; this is what lands. The Group buttons nominate the survivors while ARM is held. Tap A–H to add or drop a channel from the list, and the Group row stops reporting the mix and reports the nomination instead: full for a survivor, dim for everything else. While the modifier is down that row answers one question and no other. The list sticks between holds, so a kick-and-bass drop stays armed the way you left it. Nominate nobody and the drop refuses. It used to mute all eight, which is literally what nominating nobody means — and is how the instrument once fell silent in the middle of a take. Now it lands, changes nothing, and says so: the page indicator reads DROP 0/8 for the length you armed, which is the same “took none of eight” the timing macros use when they cannot move every channel. A macro that does nothing and does not admit it is the same fault as a silent channel that will not say why. On the landing bar every channel you did not nominate is muted. It is the mixer strip, not the sequencer — the same mute F1–F8 set — so it takes each channel's reverb and delay tail with it, and the tabs of the silenced channels draw dashed for as long as it runs. A silent channel still says why, even in the middle of a performance. The length is both numbers. Arm a drop over four bars and it fires four bars from now and lasts four bars. There is no second gesture for the duration. What comes back is exactly what was there. The mute picture is captured the instant the drop fires and restored unchanged — never "everything on". A channel you had muted by hand before the drop is still muted after it. Cancelling during a drop leaves the mutes where they are. The return is itself pending, and ERASE + SELECT cancels everything pending — so cancel mid-drop and the room stays quiet. Lift the mutes with F1–F8. BREAK — fall out now, come back on the bar BREAK is DROP with its two ends swapped. Arm it and the channels you did not nominate fall silent immediately; they come back on the bar the length names. It is the breakdown you fall into rather than build to, with the drums returning exactly on the one, counted for you. Everything else is DROP’s: the same survivors on the Group buttons, the same snapshot of who was already muted, the same restore. The length means only when it ends — there is no waiting for it to start. Only one of DROP and BREAK can be armed at a time. They share one snapshot of the mutes, so arming either drops the other. The master insert — one filter across the whole mix Put a filter on the Main chain and VOLUME → MAIN reaches it. It sits between the mixer and the card, so it hears everything: all eight channels, their reverb and delay, the drop, the ramp, everything. The factory snapshot ships with it. 018-generative-techno-main-insert is what a fresh install boots into, and it carries an MDA RezFilter on the Main chain — so the MAIN page is there from the first power-on, with no plugin to add and nothing to load. That changed on 2026-08-22; before it, the factory snapshot left the Main chain empty and the page was not built at all. 017-generative-techno is installed beside it, and it is the same instrument without the filter. Load it and the MAIN page simply is not there — VOLUME’s ring has one page fewer rather than a page of dead columns. That is the way back if the master filter ever gets in your way, and it is the reason shipping the filter by default is safe rather than a trap. In 018 the filter loads wide open and inaudible . That is deliberate rather than incidental — at the plugin’s own factory settings the cutoff sits below the point where it stops passing audio at all, so the snapshot writes every one of its controls explicitly instead of trusting a default. A plugin you add by hand does not get that treatment, so check its cutoff before you decide the rig is broken. If the instrument ever goes completely silent with every channel looking healthy, look here first and open the cutoff. It is the one control on the rig that can silence all eight channels at once, and below roughly a third of its range it is genuinely silent rather than just dark. One instance, not eight — which is why it is affordable at all. The per-channel reverb and delay sit on every chain, so an effect there costs eight times what it looks like. The reverb and the delay have pages of their own on VOLUME, and they are built the same way. Past GLOBAL and PENDING, VOLUME’s ring carries a generated page per shared effect — REV for the reverb, DLY for the delay, MAIN for the master insert when there is one — reaching every port the plugin publishes that GLOBAL does not name, with the tab row carrying parameter names instead of channels. REVTYPE and DLYFBK live there rather than on GLOBAL: one is the reverb’s own list of rooms and the other is the delay’s feedback, and each belongs beside the rest of its plugin. One turn moves that port on all eight chains at once , which is the only way a ganged effect can be steered from eight knobs. The effects this is proven on The same insert pair sits on all eight chains, so an effect costs eight times what it looks like. That is where this Pi runs out of headroom — not on the synths. Every plugin below has been measured running eight-up on this rig. Nineteen different pairs ship across the seventy-one presets , chosen for character now that the knobs find whatever is loaded. Only one pair supplies all six FX controls — TAP Stereo Echo into TAP Reverberator — so most presets give one up, and it is nearly always REVTYPE, whose 43-room list exists on that reverb alone. On a preset whose reverb already is a particular room, a room selector is redundant; that is the trade. Two others cost more and are taken deliberately: a delay that takes a normalised time cannot be locked to the grid by DLYTIME (the dub presets accept that, because feedback is the dub control), and a crossfade has no separate dry. The knobs find the effect, whatever it is Until 2026-09-04 the REVERB and DELAY encoders looked their plugin up by name, and only TAP Reverberator and TAP Stereo Echo answered. Load a snapshot with any other pair and both knobs did nothing, both kinds of modulator sat inert, and REVSIZE, REVTYPE, DLYTIME and DLYFBK were dead — with no message anywhere. It was true of twenty-one of the fifty-one genre presets and all twenty of the drone ones. The two verbs resolve by role now: the driver walks the chain and takes the first plugin that can be a reverb, and the first that can be a delay. Position is never consulted — the old packs put a reverb in the first insert slot on eight presets and a chorus in the second on four, so “slot one is the delay” would have been wrong for twelve of them. Three things this cannot fix, and the surface says so rather than pretending: REVTYPE exists on TAP Reverberator alone. Its list of 43 rooms has no counterpart on any other reverb here, so on a chain carrying a different one that column draws dead. Six of the effects below are crossfades, not sends — Shiroverb, Roomy, Modulay, GxEcho-Stereo, Regrader and Gxdigital_delay_st have no separate dry control, so turning their wet up turns the dry down. The knob is held below full travel on those, deliberately, so it cannot delete a channel’s dry signal outright. DLYTIME reaches the delays that speak milliseconds. Tal-Dub-3 and Regrader take a 0–1 delay time instead and carry their own host-sync controls, which this project has not measured — so the musical division skips those two rather than writing a number that means something else. Their feedback and wet still work. Plugin What it is TAP Reverberator algorithmic reverb, and the factory one — it has a real wet level, which is rarer than it sounds TAP Stereo Echo stereo delay, the factory partner, also a true wet send Dragonfly Hall Reverb large algorithmic hall Dragonfly Room Reverb small-room algorithmic reverb Dragonfly Early Reflections reflections only, no tail — space without wash Tal-Reverb-II / Tal-Reverb-III plate-flavoured algorithmic reverbs Shiroverb diffuse ambient reverb Roomy compact room reverb Tal-Dub-3 dub delay — filtered repeats that degrade the way tape does Regrader degrading delay: each repeat loses bits and sample rate Modulay modulated delay, chorused repeats GxEcho-Stereo stereo echo Gxdigital_delay_st clean digital stereo delay YK Chorus chorus Multivoice Chorus multi-voice chorus, thicker and slower Calf Vinyl vinyl noise, crackle and wear Calf Tape Simulator tape wow, flutter and saturation MDA RingMod ring modulator TAP AutoPanner auto-panner Ping Pong Pan ping-pong panner ZamEQ2 · 3 Band EQ parametric and three-band EQ ZamCompX2 stereo compressor What eight instances actually cost Measured on the rig at 512 frames and 48 kHz, with eight synths playing and only the insert pair changed: Insert pair Mean CPU Xruns TAP Stereo Echo + TAP Reverberator 18.5 % 0 Calf Vinyl + Tal-Reverb-III 25.4 % 0 Roomy + Tal-Reverb-II 25.8 % 0 Shiroverb + Tal-Reverb-III 28.1 % 0 Modulay + Dragonfly Hall Reverb 29.8 % 0 YK Chorus + Dragonfly Room Reverb 36.5 % 0 Five that are out, and why Plugin Measured at eight instances Aether 61.6 % with real xruns — still 49 % in the lighter three-synth layout CHOWTapeModel 82.4 % and 62 xruns ChowPhaserStereo 91.6 % — eleven of twenty-four plugin hosts never start at all Roboverb 93.8 % and 406 xruns Two Dragonfly reverbs together 52.7 %; either one alone is about 30 % Each was proven guilty by elimination — its partner in the pair measured clean elsewhere — and each was replaced in the presets that carried it. Loading without an error is not running without a glitch , which is the whole reason these numbers exist. Watch what a plugin calls a wet control. Several well-known reverbs turn out to crossfade dry against wet rather than offering a send, so turning the mix up takes the dry signal away with it. The factory pair was chosen by measuring that with an impulse, one plugin at a time. If you swap in your own, check it the same way before trusting the REVERB and DELAY encoders. What it refuses, and why Five of the eight columns draw dead under the CUTOFF lens. Only the three voices answer it. The drum channels run a sampler, and there is no filter in that chain to reach — so rather than offering a knob that would do nothing, the columns grey out. There is no drum filter in this version. That is worth saying plainly so you do not go hunting for one: filtering drums needs a filter plugin per channel, which costs eight more plugin hosts, and it has not been built. EXIT — a part that leaves rather than stops A mute is a switch. It is also the sound that gives a machine away: an arrangement made of mutes announces that somebody pressed a button, because nothing in music stops that abruptly except a fault. EXIT is encoder 8 of the AUTO page, on both kinds of channel. One setting per channel, in bars. At HARD — where everything starts — a mute is the mute you already know. Set it to 1bar or more and that channel closes instead: over the bars you asked for it gets darker and then quieter, and the part is gone by the end of the bar rather than at the instant you pressed. The gesture is one you already have. Hold MUTE and press the pad on the bottom row — the queued row, the one that has always waited for the wrap. The top row stays instant, so the grid now offers both: cut it now, or let it leave. Bringing it back works the same way and opens it again. It comes back at the level it left from. A channel you had at 40 opens again at 40, not at full, and a close that has landed leaves the fader exactly where you set it — closing a part is an arrangement gesture, and an arrangement gesture that quietly rewrote your mix would be worse than no gesture at all. The five drum channels close on level alone. They have no filter to close — their chains are the sampler, the echo and the reverb, and the only filter on the instrument sits on the main bus. The three voices get both, and the difference is audible: a voice closing sounds like a door, a drum closing sounds like a fade. That is what the instrument can honestly do today rather than a setting somebody forgot. See also Modulation — the lens is the best place to bind eight modulators at once Sound and presets — LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY per channel The surface — modes, pages, how the ring works, and the ARM gesture DROP rides on

title: Modulation

headings.text: Drift — when the pattern itself moves
RISE — a sweep that happens once
The big encoder — how much everything moves

body: Modulation Set how a value moves instead of what it is. Quick start gets you playing; this page is the second dimension underneath every knob you already know. What it is MOD is the SWING button. Hold it and every encoder stops setting a value and starts setting how that value moves . Tap it instead and it latches, so both hands are free. The button says which one you did: steady while you hold it, blinking while it is latched. Same blink GRID uses for an overridden kind, so the panel has one vocabulary and not two. It matters because a latched MOD outlives your finger — the encoders keep meaning depth and the refused columns keep their bars off until you tap it again. It is not a mode. It adds no page, no ring entry, and nothing to memorise: the map of parameters you already know does not change, and MOD gives every one of them a second dimension in the same place. It costs no plugin instances, and nothing is created or destroyed while you play. Try it Press Play and select a voice — Group G is LEAD. Press CONTROL. Encoder 2 is CUTOFF. Hold SWING — that is MOD — and turn encoder 2. The column's name gains a ~ and its bar grows a dashed span. You are setting how far the cutoff will travel, not where it sits. A small turn gives a narrow sweep; a bigger turn a broader one. Let go of SWING and listen. The filter sweeps on its own. Keep MOD held and tap pad 1 , then pad 9 . Pads 1–9 are the rates, slowest first: sixteen bars per cycle at one end, half a bar at the other. You should hear the sweep speed up dramatically between the two. Tap pads 13–16 for the four shapes — triangle, ramp, square, and sample-and-hold, which jumps to a new value each cycle and holds it there. Release MOD and turn encoder 2 again. Now you are steering the base — the centre the sweep moves around — and the sweep follows you there. Hold SWING and ERASE together and turn encoder 2. The modulation stops and the value returns to where you set it, not to wherever the sweep happened to stop. E OHAT F BASS G LEAD H PADS PRESET BA01 CUTOFF~ 0064 RESO 0032 ENV 0048 CUTOFF carries a modulator: the name gains a ~ , the bar shows the range it sweeps, and the value cell still reads the base — the number your hand owns. How it works Depth is bipolar, and centre is off. Turning back to the middle does not leave a dormant modulator behind — it removes it. The fastest way to stop something moving is to put its depth back where it started. Rates are locked to the bar , so a modulator lines up with the pattern it is colouring rather than drifting against it. Nine rates sit on the first nine pads and the four shapes on the bottom row, which leaves three pads deliberately dark in between — see below for what used to be there. The value cell always shows the base. Motion lives on the indicator bar: a dashed span across the range the modulator covers, and a small tick travelling inside it. A fast modulator blurs into a static span, and that is honest — the span is the truth, the tick is a courtesy. On 1-bit glass refreshing five times a second, animating the number would just make it unreadable. Under the lens it is eight at once. Put your hand on LEVEL, tap ALL to latch the lens on it, then tap MOD and turn each encoder in turn, and every channel gets its own modulator on the same control. They do not run in lockstep: each starts its cycle at the moment you bind it, so binding them one after another spreads them around the bar and the row breathes rather than pumps. An effect modulator is one object, not eight. The reverb and the delay are a single insert pair shared by all eight chains, so a modulator you bind on the REV, DLY or MAIN page belongs to the instrument rather than to the channel you happened to be on when you bound it. Bind it from anywhere and every channel hears it; clear it from anywhere and it is gone for all of them. This is the one place the lens has nothing to spread — there is only ever one. It is saved. Modulators go into the snapshot with their depth, rate, shape and position, and the value stored is the base you set rather than wherever the sweep happened to be. Load the set tomorrow and they are still running, still spread apart. What it refuses, and why While MOD is down, a column that will not take a modulator loses its bar — the name and the value stay, because they are still live controls; they just cannot be modulated. So you never have to remember the list: a bar means you can bind here . But the list is short enough to learn, and knowing it saves you hunting. It takes the sound. LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY on every channel; CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY on a voice; every parameter on a generated EXTRA page ; and every knob on the REV, DLY and MAIN pages. And it takes three pattern verbs — HITS, ROTATE and CHANCE. Those are drift , and they are the exception the next section is about: they move once a bar rather than continuously, and they refuse outright on a channel you have played or recorded onto. It takes nothing else. Not the rest of the pattern — DIVIDE, LENGTH, VELO, GATE, OCTAVE, RANGE, RATCHET. Not the generator’s own controls — RULE, LEAN, MODEL, MELODY, RHYTHM, LANE, MOVE, PHRASE, FILL, EXIT. Not the walk — SPAN, STRIDE, FEED, AMT. Not a name column — KIT, SAMPLE, PRESET. And not the globals — ROOT, SCALE, BPM, WALK. The refusal is the design, not a gap. A modulator writes several times a second. A knob that rewrites the pattern would tear the line up continuously — and on a channel you had recorded onto, it would destroy your take with nothing on the surface explaining why. Nothing MOD can do will touch a recorded take. Generation moving on its own is a genuinely good idea, and it does ship — but only under its own rules, which is what drift is. Drift — when the pattern itself moves Everything above modulates the sound. Drift modulates the pattern. Bind it to HITS and the channel gains and loses hits on its own; bind it to ROTATE and the bar turns under itself; bind it to CHANCE and the whole channel thins out and comes back. The arrangement evolves instead of the tone. You bind it exactly like any other modulator — hold MOD and turn HITS, ROTATE or CHANCE on the STEP page. MOD + pad sets its rate and shape as usual, and the pad legend shows them. It moves once per bar, not continuously. A pattern cannot be redrawn five times a second without tearing the groove apart, so drift waits for the pattern to come round and changes it there. At the slowest rate a full breath in and out takes about half a minute; the fastest rates change something every bar. Drift refuses to touch a channel you have recorded on, and says so. Its columns lose their bars there, exactly like any other refusal. This is the one rule that makes drift safe to leave running: a pattern rewritten with nobody touching the panel would otherwise erase your take while you played. If you record onto a channel that is already drifting, the drift stops. It is checked every bar, not only when you bind it, so your take is safe the moment it exists. The drift is not thrown away — hand the channel back with ERASE + Group and it picks up where it left off. The pads become the menu While MOD is down the sixteen pads stop showing your pattern and show the modulation menu instead. They were always the menu — a pad hit under MOD has always set a rate or a shape — they just used to keep drawing steps while they did it. Now they say what they are. Pads 1–9 are the rates , slower on the left, faster to the right and down. The bottom row is the four shapes — triangle, ramp, square, and sample-and-hold. Pads 10, 11 and 12 are dark and do nothing , and that is not an oversight: three faster rates lived there and were removed because they could not produce the shape they named. The shapes stayed on the bottom row rather than sliding up into the gap, so every rate and every shape is still on the pad it was always on. The pads used to fade, each at its own rate and in its own shape, so you could see what a setting felt like before choosing it. That is gone, for the same reason the tick is — repainting sixteen pads on a timer floods the connection the buttons come back on. The grid is still now, and the rate you have chosen is named on the label. The rate and shape you are using are lit full , brighter than the rest, so what is selected reads at a glance. If every pad is dim and still, nothing is bound yet. MOD + pad only has something to act on once a modulator exists, so rather than dance under a gesture that would do nothing, the pads say so. Bind one — MOD and turn any encoder with a bar — and the menu comes alive. That is also what you get straight after loading a snapshot, even one full of modulators. The menu edits the modulator you last bound, and loading a set gives you modulators nobody bound this session — they are running, they are in the snapshot, and none of them is the one this menu is pointed at. Turn any encoder with a bar under MOD and the menu is live again on that one. There is no playhead here: under MOD the pads are not steps, so a sweep would point at nothing. Let MOD go and your pattern comes straight back. The rates span thirty-two to one — the slowest is over half a minute per cycle, the fastest just under a second. Further right and further down is faster; the label tells you exactly which one you are on. Three faster rates were removed, and it is worth knowing why they were never real. Modulation is written a few times a second, so a cycle has to last several times that to be a shape rather than a stutter. The three fastest were a quarter of a bar, an eighth and a sixteenth — about half a second, a quarter and an eighth of one — which is one or two writes per cycle. They were on the pad grid, lit like everything else, and what came out was not the triangle or the ramp you asked for; it was whatever those one or two writes happened to land on, and it changed from bar to bar. Anything already saved keeps the rate it had , because the surviving rates never moved off their pads; a set saved on one of the three that went comes back on the fastest one that remains, and says so in the log rather than falling silent. RISE — a sweep that happens once A modulator normally cycles for ever. Hold ARM — that is SELECT — and tap a shape pad, and it sweeps once and stays where it ends. That is the riser: the cutoff climbs over eight bars and sits at the top instead of falling back down. It acts on the modulator you bound most recently , which is the same one MOD + pad has always steered. MOD latches, so there is no chord to catch: tap MOD, then hold ARM and tap pads 13–16. SHIFT still outranks both — a pad under SHIFT is a step's odds, whatever else is latched. Where it holds depends on the shape you tap , because holding at the end of one sweep is not the same place for all four: Pad Shape Once, it 13 triangle rises, falls, and holds at the bottom 14 ramp climbs all the way and holds at the top — this is the riser 15 square jumps to the top for the first half, drops, and holds at the bottom 16 sample-and-hold picks one value and holds it for the whole sweep Under a one-shot the rate pads mean length. Pads 1–9 are the same nine numbers, sixteen bars down to half a bar, read as how long the whole sweep takes rather than how long one cycle takes. Tapping one restarts the sweep from that moment at the new length — which is also how you fire the same riser again. The sweep starts when you tap, not on the next downbeat. It runs for the length you chose from that instant and then holds, so aim the tap, or arm a long one and let it arrive. Nothing on the panel marks a modulator as one-shot. The column keeps its ~ and its dashed span and the pads keep their menu. You hear it rather than see it: the sweep arrives and stays there instead of coming back. It refuses exactly what MOD refuses. Running once is a shape, not a new permission: the pattern-rewriting columns still have no bar, and drift still refuses a channel you have recorded on. A one-shot is not saved as one. Reload the set and that modulator is cycling again — hold ARM and tap its shape pad to make it one-shot once more. To turn one back into a cycle without reloading, clear it with MOD + ERASE and that encoder, then bind it again. Clearing everything at once Hold MOD and ERASE and press ALL . Every modulator goes, and every value lands back where you put it. The markers vanish the instant you press it; the values themselves settle a moment later. That gap is deliberate — the instrument will not write twenty parameters inside a single button press, because doing that on the button thread once froze the whole machine. The big encoder — how much everything moves While MOD is latched, the big encoder scales every live modulator at once , from nothing up to about twice their set depth. One hand takes a static rig to a churning one and back. Every modulated column’s dashed span widens and narrows together as you turn, which is the most literal picture of what is happening. Turn it down to zero and everything parks; turn it back and every modulator returns to exactly the depth you gave it — the multiplier is kept separately rather than multiplied into the depths, so nothing is stranded at zero with no way back. This is the one exception to the big encoder being the page ring. While MOD is latched it is the depth knob instead. MOD’s own label on the page indicator is what tells you which of the two you are holding. The label carries the multiplier too, as soon as it is not 1. MOD 4 BARS x0.84 means every modulator is running at 84 per cent of the depth you gave it. At 1 nothing is shown, because 1 is the absence of a setting rather than a setting. It matters because this is a knob with no end stops in the middle: turning out and back by hand does not return you to exactly where you were, and without a number nothing would ever tell you that everything on the rig is moving less than you think it is. Sweeps start with the phrase Every modulator counts from the phrase, not from when the instrument was switched on. An eight-bar sweep is the eight bars rather than an eight-bar sweep at some arbitrary offset, and starting the transport or pressing RESTART re-zeros the whole modulation system along with the bar count. The relative spread between modulators is kept, so eight LFOs that were chasing each other go on chasing each other. The pump — MOD + RESTART The bar-synced gain movement that glues a techno mix is not a separate feature here. It is a modulator on LEVEL with a negative depth: bind one on each channel and every strip ducks and recovers in time. The problem was never the sound, it was the phase. Binding eight of them one after another gives you eight modulators each starting from the moment you bound it, so they duck at eight different times and the mix sounds smeared rather than pumped. Hold MOD and press RESTART. Every modulator jumps to the start of its cycle together, and from then on they move as one. Bare RESTART deliberately does not do this. It restarts the patterns and re-zeros the bar count, and it leaves your sweeps running. A sixteen-bar filter sweep should not snap back because you restarted a loop — when you reach for RESTART you are asking about the pattern. Hold MOD and you are asking about modulation, and that is exactly when the answer changes. The shape, on the screen The pads tell you how fast a modulator moves — that is what you pick from when you bind one. Nothing told you what shape it was, so a column with a tilde beside its name could have been a triangle or a square and you had to remember which pad you pressed. A bound column now draws a small picture of its wave in the name row, beside the tilde: the rise of a ramp, the peak of a triangle, the two levels of a square, the steps of sample-and-hold. It is a silhouette rather than a plot — enough to tell them apart at a glance, which is the whole question. It does not move. It is redrawn when you change the shape and at no other time. A picture that animated the wave would repaint both screens many times a second, and that is exactly what once took this controller off the USB bus mid-jam. title: Performing

headings.text: The phrase — one bar count for the whole instrument
ARM — landing a change on a bar
PENDING — what is armed, and how to kill one
The mute grid — arrangement by pad
Beat repeat — squeeze it to one beat
Gate collapse — the notes tighten into the landing
The bank grid — sixteen arrangements under one button

body: Performing Everything that lands on a boundary rather than under your finger: the bar count the whole instrument shares, the macros you arm against it, the two grids that rearrange the set, and the two ways of holding the machine still. These are the controls you reach for while the music is running and your eyes are somewhere else. They have one thing in common and it is worth saying before any of them: almost nothing here happens the moment you press it. A drop, a bank, a queued mute and a reroll all wait for a boundary, because a change arriving mid-bar is a change that trips the groove. What you get instead of immediacy is a countdown you can read and, nearly always, a second press that takes it back. The panel itself — the four modes, the lens, the duration rule and what the lights mean — is on The surface . This page assumes it. The phrase — one bar count for the whole instrument The page name on the display carries a bar number — STEP 5/16 — counting one to sixteen and starting again. It is one count for all eight channels, not one per channel. Each channel owns its own length, so eight channels can be on eight different bars; a count taken from any one of them would be a lie on the other seven. This one comes from the transport instead, so it stays true however far apart the lengths are — see lengths that do not agree . The count corrects itself against the music, every bar. It is worked out from tempo and the system clock, while the sequencer runs on the audio clock — two time bases for the same number, and they were measured drifting far enough apart to lose a whole bar every eight minutes, which put every armed macro progressively late in a long set. Each bar the count now takes back a quarter of the gap, gently enough that nothing you are reading ever jumps. Measured after the change: a bar of slip would take about a month. Which of the two was wrong is now known, and it is the sequencer. Zynthian rounds one sequencer tick down to a whole audio frame and never gives the remainder back, so at most tempi you play slightly faster than you asked — ask for 124 and you get 124.48. The count above no longer cares, because it corrects against the sequencer rather than against the tempo. But it does mean the number on the touchscreen need not be the number you are playing , which matters the moment you run alongside anything else. Some tempi come out exact, and the instrument now ships on one. At 48 kHz the rounding vanishes whenever the tempo divides 30000 — 100, 120 , 125 , 150 , 200. It is not gradual: 124 drifts a bar clear of nominal every eight minutes, while 125, where the factory snapshot now starts, is perfect. Stay on one of those and the touchscreen number is the truth. Move off and nothing inside the instrument minds — only outside gear does. Bar 1 is the moment you press Play, and Restart re-zeros it along with the playheads — count and patterns are pulled back onto the one together. Stop and the number goes away rather than freezing, because a stuck number reads as a clock that has died. It is a live ruler, not a position: it is not saved, and it starts again from one on the next Play. Hold NAVIGATE and the sixteen pads become the phrase , one pad per bar: the bars behind you dim, the bar you are in full, the bars ahead dark. With the transport stopped every pad is dark. Let go and your pattern comes straight back. While NAVIGATE is up, the pads are a readout and nothing else. A pad hit does not toggle a step, does not play the channel, does nothing at all — the surface takes the press and drops it. This is the one overlay that is purely a display, so you can read the phrase page mid–bar without your hand costing you anything. The count is read thirty times a second, so anything scheduled against it lands within a few hundredths of a bar. That is close enough for a mute or a level, and deliberately not close enough for anything that has to sit on a step. ARM — landing a change on a bar SELECT is ARM. Hold it and compose two things on the pads: what is going to happen, and how many bars away . Tap it instead and the grid stays, like every other modifier here. Pads while ARM is held What they are 1–7 the macro — DROP , CHANCE ramp , HALF , DOUBLE , BREAK , ratchet ramp , gate collapse . Amber, and the one you picked lights full 8 dark, and it does nothing. This is where a later macro goes 9–16 the length in bars — 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16. Green The page indicator says what you have picked. While ARM is held it reads ARM? until you touch a macro pad, then ARM DROP , ARM THIN , ARM HALF , ARM DOUBLE , ARM BREAK , ARM ROLL or ARM TIGHT . Seven amber pads look alike in a dark room; the label is how you know which one your thumb found. It goes away the moment you release ARM, because from then on the countdown, the SELECT light and the PENDING page carry it. Pick the macro first, then the length. The length is the commit: tapping it arms the macro. A length on its own does nothing at all, because guessing which macro you meant would fire something you never named. The grid becomes a countdown the instant something is armed. One red pad per bar of the length you chose, going out from the top left as the bars pass, so the pads still lit are the bars still to come. While that is showing every pad is inert — reading the countdown must not also change it. ERASE + SELECT cancels everything pending. That is the panic gesture, and it cancels all rather than one for the same reason a reroll does: a half-cancelled gesture is harder to think about mid-bar than none. It sits on ERASE because ERASE is this instrument’s one word for taking something away, and it rhymes with the surgical version — ERASE and the encoder under a single column on the PENDING page. Reading the countdown is safe. Any release used to cancel everything, however long you had held it — so the only way to look at the ruler destroyed what you were looking at. Now a release does nothing at all, and a tap leaves the grid up so you can keep reading it with your hand back on a knob. Freeze the machine and the countdown holds with it. The pads stop going out, the number stops falling, and the PENDING page swaps its digits for HELD . Nothing armed is lost — it lands on the first bar after you thaw. Without this the count ran to zero and sat there advertising a drop that could not land, which is the one reading a countdown must never give. SELECT is the indicator once your hand has left it. Dim when nothing is armed, one pulse per bar while a macro counts down, and steady through the bar it lands on. The pulse is driven by the bar count rather than by a timer, so it cannot drift away from the thing it is counting — and it is the one place on this panel where a moving light does not mean latched. A countdown and a modifier cannot share one LED, and the countdown is the one you need from across a room. Arming with the transport stopped keeps the length and waits. There is no bar to count from yet, so nothing can fire; press Play and the macro lands that many bars in. SELECT sits steady rather than flashing meanwhile, because nothing is counting down yet. Arming a macro that is already pending replaces it instead of stacking a second one, so two drops can never land on different bars and fight over the same restore. With MOD active, ARM belongs to the modulators instead. MOD latches, so MOD held or latched plus ARM is the gesture that makes a modulator sweep once — see RISE . Tap MOD off first if you want to arm a macro. SHIFT outranks both : a pad under SHIFT is a step's odds, whatever else is latched. BREAK is the exception to the length. Every other macro fires in N bars; BREAK fires immediately and comes back in N. There is no “in N bars” for a gesture whose whole point is that it happens now. DROP and BREAK cannot both be armed. They are the same mechanism with its ends swapped and they share one snapshot of who was muted, so arming either quietly drops the other. Only one thing may own the mutes at a time. Each macro is written up where it lands: DROP and BREAK , the CHANCE ramp , HALF and DOUBLE , and the ratchet ramp . PENDING — what is armed, and how to kill one Press VOLUME and step to its second page. One column per armed macro, soonest first, with the bars remaining and a bar counting down. With nothing armed it says NONE rather than drawing eight blank columns. Hold ERASE and turn the encoder under a column to cancel that one. ERASE + SELECT still cancels everything — that is the panic gesture. This is the surgical version, and the two share a modifier because they are the same verb at two sizes. The columns are sorted by how soon each lands and only move when something really overtakes something else, so the page stays readable while it counts. Every macro shows up twice — once going out, once coming back. The names are short enough for a column head, so learn the twelve of them: DROP and UNDROP , BREAK and UNBREAK , HALF or DOUBLE and their RETURN , ROLL and UNROLL for the ratchet ramp, TIGHT and UNTIGHT for gate collapse, and THIN for the CHANCE ramp. THIN is the one that does not match its name elsewhere in this guide: the ramp is called CHANCE where you arm it and THIN where it counts down, because it is thinning the bar out. FREEZE — stop the machine evolving PAD MODE is FREEZE, and it has two depths. Gesture What holds still Tap — latches MELODY, RHYTHM, drift, reroll, FILL, the armed macro queue and the chord walker — everything that would rewrite a pattern or move the key on its own . The notes stop changing under you, the key stops moving, the fourth bar stops answering — and the LFOs keep sweeping , so the sound goes on breathing Hold — momentary all of that plus the LFOs. Everything parks until you let go That is the surface’s standing rule — a tap latches, a hold is momentary — so there is nothing new to learn. Tap again to thaw. A frozen instrument says so three times over , because one that did not would read as a broken one: PAD MODE lights, the page indicator gains FRZ (or FRZ! for the total hold), and the MELODY and RHYTHM columns lose their bars in the same grey MOD already uses for “this control cannot act right now”. The values stay — they are what resumes. The light tells the two depths apart the way the whole panel does: blinking for the latched, shallow freeze, steady bright while you hold the total one. A pending reroll is held, not thrown away. Its tab stays dashed and it fires on the next wrap after you thaw. SHIFT + PAD MODE used to be a trapdoor, and is not one any more. That combination never reaches the instrument — the USB daemon eats it — and until 3 September 2026 the daemon used it to step into a sixteen-step sequencer of its own, where the pads stopped sending notes, PLAY and STOP drove its transport, the Group buttons changed its pages, and every pad LED was repainted in its colour. Nothing on the panel said so, and the way out was three more presses of the same chord. That sequencer is now off unless internal_sequencer in maschine.json asks for it, so the chord is simply swallowed and nothing happens. Nothing else about FREEZE changed. Read The mute grid — arrangement by pad Hold MUTE and the sixteen pads become your eight channels, twice. Tap it instead and the grid stays, which is what you want when you are going to work the arrangement for a while and need the hand back. Pads while MUTE is held What they do Top two rows, 1–8 mute and unmute channel A–H now Bottom two rows, 9–16 queue the same change to that channel’s next wrap Each pad wears its channel’s own colour, because hue is identity everywhere on this surface. Full means audible, dark means muted. A pad in the bottom half shows the change, not the state : half-lit when something is queued for that channel and dark when nothing is. Drawing the state there would only repeat the row above. Tap a queued pad twice and the queue is cancelled rather than reversed — the second press of a gesture is its undo everywhere else here. Pressing the instant pad also clears anything queued for that channel, so one strip never has two answers waiting. It is the mixer strip that mutes, the same one the F row uses, so it is in your snapshot and shows on the touchscreen mixer. Beat repeat — squeeze it to one beat Hold the transport’s ▶ STEP button. Every generated channel collapses to its first beat and loops it; let go and the patterns come straight back. One beat is the floor — a pattern’s length is whole beats and always will be, so there is no half-bar repeat. Worth knowing that a beat is a different size per channel: at 1/4 it is a single step, at 1/32 it is eight. The same gesture is a repeated hit on a coarse channel and a tight stutter on a fine one. Channels you have recorded onto are skipped , and the page indicator says how many it took — RPT6 means six of the eight. A take has no generator settings to rebuild it from afterwards, so collapsing one would lose it. Gate collapse — the notes tighten into the landing The seventh macro on ARM, on pad 7. Arm it and, over the bars you chose, every note gets shorter — the groove goes tight and dry without a filter moving — and then everything returns to the length it had. It is the cheapest way to build tension this instrument has, because nothing about the pattern changes: the same steps play, they just stop sooner. Ratchets survive it, which is worth knowing, because collapse rebuilds each pattern from a capture and a rebuild is exactly where a roll could quietly go missing. The bank grid — sixteen arrangements under one button The sequencer has sixty-four banks and this instrument has always used one. A bank is a complete eight-channel pattern set, so a bank is a scene : every channel’s pattern at once. Hold DUPLICATE , or tap it and it stays. The pads become sixteen banks, and the big encoder walks the four pages of them — the label reads BANK 1/4 and then which bank you are in. A press lands on the bar, so tapping the modifier is the useful half here: your hand is free while you wait for the boundary. What the colours mean: One bright pad — the bank you are playing. Dimmer pads of the same colour — banks that exist and hold something. A green pad — a bank you have asked for. It arrives at the bar. Dark — nothing there yet. A press lands on the bar, never under your finger. A whole arrangement arriving mid-bar is the one gesture on this instrument that could not possibly be in time. Press the queued bank again to cancel it, which is what a second press means everywhere else here. Pressing a dark pad makes that bank. It arrives blank — eight empty channels laid out the way this instrument expects — and you build it from there. This is deliberate: left to itself the sequencer would have invented a sixteen-pad grid on the wrong MIDI channels and written it into your snapshot. A snapshot now saves every bank, and comes back on the one you saved it on. Both halves of that were missing until recently and the older behaviour is worth knowing, because a set saved under it will still load that way: the patterns of every bank were always saved, but the generator settings of the banks you were not playing were not, so the other banks came back with fresh settings rather than the ones you left them with. HITS and ROTATE were the worst of it — those two also leaked between banks while you switched, so a rotation you set in one bank followed you into the next and was gone from the one you left. Neither of those numbers can be worked out from the pattern afterwards , which is why they mattered more than they look. A rotated line sounds rotated but nothing can measure how far it was turned, and once a rhythm register is thinning a line the instrument deliberately refuses to guess HITS back out of what is left. If the instrument does not remember them, nothing does. A bank you have never visited is still blank , and that has not changed — it is the honest answer, not a gap. A bank that never held settings does not acquire them from whichever bank you happened to launch it from. And a set saved on bank 3 loads on bank 3. The sequencer always comes back on bank 1 whatever it was saved on, so a multi-bank set used to load bank 1's patterns underneath bank 3's settings — silently, because both halves looked entirely normal. If the bank a snapshot names is not in the file, the instrument stays where it landed and says so in the log rather than inventing an empty one. See also The surface — the panel these gestures are made on Generating patterns — what a reroll is actually rerolling Modulation — RISE, the one-shot sweep armed the same way Saving your work — what a snapshot keeps of all this

title: Playing and recording

headings.text: Editing a take, step by step
Capturing the jam to a file
Pressing harder — the pads are pressure-sensitive

body: Playing and recording The pads are the instrument. Hold REC while you play them and what you played is captured into the same pattern the generator writes — and from that moment the pattern is yours, not the machine's. What it is In CONTROL, AUTO and VOLUME the sixteen pads play the selected channel. On a voice they are notes. On a drum every pad triggers that channel's own sound, because a drum channel is one sound — hearing CLAP while playing KICK would be the silent-channel confusion in a new costume. In STEP the pads are the step editor instead. A tap toggles that step, and the velocity of the tap becomes the step's velocity, so accents are played in rather than dialled. Step 0 is the top-left pad; the grid reads left to right, top to bottom. Hold ERASE and a pad deletes that step rather than toggling it. On a step that is already empty it does nothing at all — the difference matters when you are clearing a run of pads by feel and do not want the empty ones switching on behind your hand. And it stays deleted. On a channel the machine is generating, an erased step used to come straight back the next time anything made the machine write the pattern again — a turn of HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE, LENGTH or RHYTHM, a reroll, or just a channel drifting on its own. The erase now goes into the same register a tap writes to, so it survives all of that. On a channel you recorded, your notes were always the truth and it always removed them properly. Try it Press Play , select Group F (BASS) and press CONTROL . Play the pads — that is the instrument. Hold REC and play a short phrase. Keep holding REC. Let go of the last pad while REC is still held , then release REC. Your phrase is in the pattern. Press STEP and look at the pads. The steps you played light amber . On a voice they are the only steps lit — your take replaced the generated line. On a drum the generated hits are still there underneath, dim or bright. Look at the page indicator. It reads PLAY — you own this pattern now, and the generator has stopped rewriting it. To give it back: hold ERASE and press Group F . Your take is gone and the generator resumes. That is deliberate and it is destructive. How it works Capture happens on release, not on press. A note's length is how long you held the pad, and that is not known until you let go. This has a consequence worth committing to memory: you must still be holding REC when you release the pad. Let go of REC first and the note sounds but is never captured. That is the same rule that lets you release REC without cutting off notes still ringing, so it is a trade rather than an oversight. Strikes quantise to the nearest step , wrapping at the end of the bar — nearest rather than next, so a strike landing a hair early is not pushed a step late. A note's length is clamped to what is left of the pattern. On a voice, your take replaces the line. On a drum, it goes on top. The first captured note on a voice clears what the Turing generator had written, so what you hear afterwards is your phrase and nothing else — which is what makes a recorded voice sound like a part rather than two parts at once. Nothing is lost that cannot come back: hold ERASE and press that channel's Group button and the generator rebuilds its line from the same register it always had. A drum keeps both. Its hits are euclidean and a recorded strike on top of them is an accent, so the generated pattern freezes where it is and your note joins it — a recorded step there can hold two notes, and an amber pad means your note is present and the generated one still is. A step that sounds but stays dark would be the defect. The page indicator reads REC while you are capturing , and REC-STOP if the transport is stopped — nothing is being captured then, and the surface says so rather than letting you play into nothing. Who owns the pattern The first captured note makes you the owner of that channel's pattern, and the generator stops rewriting it. The indicator reads PLAY for as long as that holds — including after a snapshot reload , because ownership is saved. Handing the pattern back is deliberate and destructive: your take is gone the moment it happens. There are two routes, and knowing which knobs do it is the difference between keeping a take and losing one. Route On a drum On a voice Gesture ERASE + the channel's Group button Knobs that hand back HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE, LEAN, LANE, RHYTHM LENGTH, DIVIDE, MELODY, RHYTHM Knobs that keep the take LENGTH, VELO, CHANCE, SWING GATE, OCTAVE, CHANCE, SWING Two of a voice’s knobs go dark on a take instead: RANGE and VELO. Both are read only when the generator writes a line, and it does not write a take — so they used to move a number on the screen and change nothing you could hear. They draw ---- now and their encoders do nothing, which is the honest version of what was already happening. GATE and OCTAVE stay live and are worth knowing why: GATE is the length of a step you tap in by hand , and OCTAVE decides what a pad plays , take or no take. LEAN, LANE and RHYTHM joined the drum list on 2 September, and they were missing rather than exempt. All three ask the generator for a different pattern, so like HITS and ROTATE they cannot leave a take standing — but they used to take it without saying so : the notes were replaced and the channel still called itself yours. They hand back like the others now, and the indicator stops reading PLAY the moment they do. Turning one of them down to nothing — LANE to RAW , RHYTHM to LOCK , LEAN back to OFF — asks the generator for nothing, so it keeps the take. Two details worth carrying: a drum's LENGTH keeps the take, because shortening a pattern preserves the steps that still fit; and MELODY and RHYTHM only hand back when they move off LOCK , since a locked generator rewrites nothing and could not undo your recording anyway. A knob has to actually move — brushing one does nothing. On a drum channel the amber colouring does not survive a snapshot reload, and that is not a lost take. A played drum note carries the same pitch as a generated one, so once the pattern is read back there is nothing left to tell the two apart. The notes are all there and the channel is still yours: the indicator still reads PLAY , and after a reload that indicator, not the pad colour, is the authority. On a voice the amber usually survives, because the played pitch is normally its own. The exception is worth knowing: if the note you play happens to be the very note the generator would have put on that step, the two are indistinguishable once the pattern is read back, and that step returns in the group colour like a drum. The take is intact either way — the PLAY indicator remains the authority. Editing a take, step by step On a channel you own, the pads in STEP mode edit the pattern itself. Tap an empty step and a note appears there; tap a step that sounds and it goes. Nothing else in the pattern moves — the note you recorded four steps earlier is exactly where you left it. That is not what a tap does on a channel the machine owns, and the difference is the whole idea. There, a tap is a message to the generator : it marks the step as one you want used, and the line is rewritten around it. On a take there is no generator to send a message to, so the tap does the obvious thing instead. You tap What happens an empty step a note is added, at the nearest note your take already uses — so it stays in the material you played rather than borrowing a pitch from the generator a step that sounds it is removed. A chord goes as a chord , all of its notes at once ERASE + a step the same removal, and the same whole-chord rule Your tap’s velocity is the note’s accent , so a hard tap is a loud step. And an added note is shortened if it would otherwise run into the next step that sounds, which is the same rule the generator writes under. One thing to expect: a step you tap in draws in the channel’s colour rather than amber when the note you added happens to be the note the generator would have put there. That is the same limit described above — nothing in the pattern records who wrote a note — and the PLAY indicator remains the authority on whose channel it is. Capturing the jam to a file SHIFT + REC starts and stops an audio recording. It captures the master — all eight channels, the effects, and anything a macro does to them — to a WAV on the Pi, alongside the other captures. It cannot collide with overdub, which is bare REC held . That is also why it is a chord rather than a long press: a long press of REC already is the overdub hold. REC’s light tells you which one you are in. Dim when a take is possible, full while you hold it for an overdub, and red while a recording is being written — including when you have moved to a page where overdub is not possible, so a running capture can never be invisible. The pad colours, in full Nothing on the pads is decorative. Without a modifier held they are the pattern of the selected channel, in that channel’s own colour — warm for the drums, cool for the voices, the same colour as its Group button. What you see What it is the channel’s colour, full a step that fires the channel’s colour, barely lit a step that is empty dark past the end of the pattern — this is how you read LENGTH off the grid white, moving the playhead amber a step you played in yourself — on a voice, after a take, every lit step is one of yours Every modifier that claims the pads replaces this picture for as long as it is held or latched, and hands it straight back: SHIFT shows each step’s odds, MOD the rates and shapes, ARM the macros and the countdown, MUTE the eight channels, DUPLICATE the sixteen banks, NAVIGATE the phrase — and under NAVIGATE alone a pad press does nothing at all, because a bar of the phrase is not a step. Each is written up where that gesture is. What it refuses, and why You cannot record in STEP mode — there the pads belong to the step editor, which on a channel you own edits your take directly — and you cannot record while MOD is active , where they pick a modulator's rate and shape. In both cases the REC button is unlit — unless an audio capture is running, which outranks everything and keeps it red. A lit REC would otherwise be promising a take it cannot make, so it goes dark rather than letting you play a phrase into nothing and wonder why it vanished. Pressing harder — the pads are pressure-sensitive The pads have measured how hard you are pressing since 2015, continuously, the whole time a pad is held. The instrument now listens. Hold a pad on a voice channel and squeeze: the filter opens, proportionally, for as long as you press. Let go and it eases back to wherever your CUTOFF knob is set. The knob keeps working while a squeeze is live — the squeeze is an offset over your setting, not a replacement for it. Two deliberate limits. It acts on voice channels only ; on a drum it does nothing, because the drum chains have no filter to open. And the number on the screen does not move while you press : it shows where your knob is, which is where the sound returns to. A value that chased your finger would be an animation, and animating a number on these screens is how you overload the connection to the controller. The range was measured across all sixteen pads rather than assumed: a firm press reaches about four fifths of what the hardware nominally reports, so the scaling is set to that rather than to the theoretical maximum. A hard squeeze reaches the top of the filter. Note velocity is untouched by this — how hard a pad sounds when you hit it works exactly as it did. See also Generating patterns — what you are playing over Modulation — why nothing MOD does can touch a recorded take The surface — every button and light, and what to check when it goes quiet

title: Saving your work

headings.text: What it will not carry, and why
Putting a snapshot on an exact tempo
Generating starting points of your own

body: Saving your work A snapshot holds the whole instrument — patterns, sounds, levels, and the driver's own state. Two things it cannot hold, and one trap in the web interface. Try it On the touchscreen (or through VNC in a browser), open the snapshot list and enter a bank. The first entry is Save as new snapshot . That is the one. To load, pick any snapshot in the list. Everything comes back — including which channels you had switched, and who owned each pattern. The trap In webconf's Snapshots page, the Name field and its checkmark RENAME THE SELECTED BANK. They do not save a snapshot. It looks exactly like a save box. It is not one. Save from the touchscreen or VNC. What a snapshot carries The patterns themselves, play chance and swing, mixer levels and mutes, both effect sends per channel, and each channel's kit or preset. Plus the driver's own state, which exists nowhere else: every voice's Turing register and its four-deep undo ring, the voice parameters, the globals, which channels you switched kind on , who owns each pattern , your modulators — depth, rate, shape, position and base — and the mode and page you were in. A set saved mid-sweep comes back at the value you dialled in, not wherever a modulator happened to be when you saved. What it will not carry, and why A mute set on the sequencer does not persist. Mute the mixer strip instead — that is in the snapshot, and it shows on the touchscreen mixer too. The phrase count and anything armed are not saved. The bar count is a live ruler rather than a position — it starts again from one on the next Play — and a macro still counting down is gone with it. A one-shot modulator comes back cycling, and a set saved while a drop is running saves those mutes, because mixer mutes are exactly what a snapshot does carry. Amber provenance on a drum channel does not survive a reload. Your take does; the colour does not. A played drum note has the same pitch as a generated one, so once the pattern is read back nothing can tell them apart. The PLAY indicator remains the authority. Taking your patterns elsewhere A snapshot holds the eight patterns, and a small tool that ships with the project writes them out as an ordinary MIDI file you can open in anything: python3 tools/export-patterns-midi.py snapshot/018-generative-techno-main-insert.zss You get one file: a tempo track, then a track per channel, each on its own MIDI channel and named for its group. It reads the saved snapshot rather than the running instrument, so it takes nothing from the rig — you can run it while you are playing, or with the instrument switched off entirely. Two things it deliberately does not carry, so that nothing in the file is invented: Note lengths. Every note comes out one step long. The length the sequencer stores is not consistent between a drum and a voice, and it never had to be — the drum sounds are one-shots that play to the end of the sample whichever way you ask, and a voice’s notes are rewritten when the snapshot loads. A uniform gate you are told about is worth more than a length guessed from a field nobody has decoded. Per-note chance. A step that plays four times in five is not something a MIDI file can express, so it is written as a note that always plays. What you get is the pattern as it would sound with every chance turned up. Putting a snapshot on an exact tempo The phrase page explains why a handful of tempos are exact on this hardware and the rest run a few parts per million fast. If you want one of your own snapshots moved onto an exact one, there is a tool for it: python3 tools/set-snapshot-tempo.py --tempo 125 snapshot/my-set.zss Do not edit the file by hand. A snapshot carries the tempo in two places — the sequencer's own riff and the surface's saved globals — and writing one without the other gives you a set whose display and whose playback disagree. The tool writes both, then reads the file back, puts both fields where they were, and refuses unless the result is byte–identical to what it started with. That proves the tempo is the only thing that moved. Generating starting points of your own The genre pack is built from a plain list of snapshot descriptions. A second tool lets you write one of those descriptions as ranges rather than numbers — a tempo somewhere in the low 130s, a filter somewhere open — and draw as many concrete variants from it as you want, or blend two existing styles into a third: python3 tools/style-sampler.py sample --style snapshot/example-style.json --variants 4 --seed 1234 --out /tmp/sampled.json python3 tools/style-sampler.py blend --manifest snapshot/genre-pack-manifest.json --a 031-house-classic --b 046-minimal-dry --t 0.5 --out /tmp/blend.json What comes out is an ordinary description list, which the normal pack builder turns into .zss files with no change at all. The seed is part of the command, so the same seed gives you the same set of variants tomorrow — a style you liked is a number you can write down. It runs on a computer, never on the instrument : nothing on the rig can read a range, and a knob that could show one has nowhere to put it on a 256×64 screen. See also Playing and recording — what ownership means, and why amber matters Modulation — modulators are saved running

title: Sound and presets

headings.text: The synth engines this is proven on

body: Sound and presets What each channel sounds like, how to change it while the rig plays, and how to make a channel behave as something its engine is not. What it is CONTROL is the sound page, and it follows the engine. A drum engine gives you KIT, SAMPLE and RANGE; a synth engine gives you PRESET, CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY. Encoders 6, 7 and 8 are LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY on every channel — the same three controls in the same place, always. The engine decides, not the behaviour. A sampler played by the Turing register still has a kit and a sample, so it still shows them. Switching a channel's kind changes how it is played, never what it is. Every channel keeps its engine for the life of the snapshot. Nothing is created or destroyed while you play, because building a plugin rebuilds the audio graph and that is a hole in the sound. Try it Select Group A (KICK) and press CONTROL . Encoder 1 is KIT, encoder 2 is SAMPLE. Turn SAMPLE. The kick changes to another sound inside the same kit, immediately. Press the button to the right of the big encoder. Same effect — it steps the selected channel's sound without using an encoder. Hold SHIFT and press it again. Now it steps the kit rather than the sample. Only a drum engine has kits, so on a synth channel this does nothing. Select Group G (LEAD) and press CONTROL . Now encoder 1 is PRESET and encoders 2–5 are CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY. Turn CUTOFF. You are driving the synth that is actually loaded, not a fixed idea of one. Now the interesting one. Select Group E (OHAT) and hold SHIFT while pressing GRID . The channel changes what it behaves as. Do it again to change back. One channel arrives switched E · OHAT ships as a voice. It keeps its Simmons kit and its sampler, but the Turing register drives it rather than euclid, so it walks between samples instead of laying down a straight hat. If your open hat wanders and you did not ask it to, that is the factory state and not a fault . Press SHIFT + GRID on E to hear it as an ordinary euclidean hat. It ships that way so the switch is audible the moment you plug in. How switching a kind works SHIFT + GRID switches the selected channel between drum and voice behaviour. The engine is never swapped. A drum kit gets the Turing generator, and a synth gets euclid. On a sampler the register walks the kit's own note list rather than ROOT and SCALE, because there a note selects a sample and scale-quantising would land most steps on empty keys — silence with nothing to explain it. On a synth, euclid becomes a root pulse : ROOT plus that channel's OCTAVE, on every hit. Each channel keeps a separate set of parameters per kind, so switching back and forth does not cost you your settings. Pattern length and division deliberately do not move: they are pattern time, not kind, and the groove must not jump under a switch. The surface says when a channel is not itself. The page indicator reads VOX or DRM , and GRID blinks for as long as the selected channel is on an overridden kind. Switching back clears the override rather than pinning the channel to a kind it merely happens to have today — so a later snapshot putting a different engine on that chain is not overruled by a stale choice nobody remembers making. What it refuses, and why A switch rewrites the pattern , so on a channel you have recorded onto it hands the pattern back to the generator and your take is gone. Hand-edited steps do not survive either, for the same reason turning HITS does not — switching rewrites the line from the generator. A voice switched to drum may arrive silent , because its HITS can read back as 0. The tab draws dashed to say so. That is not a defect: turn HITS up. A defect that was published here has been withdrawn. The buttons beside the big encoder were reported to step a preset once and then stick. They never did: they step every press. What stuck was the name . The value was drawn in a font that fits four characters, and preset banks are full of neighbours that agree on their first four — a padthv1 bank of 67 patches has six called Dusk , Dusk2 … Dusk6 , and stepping walks a bank alphabetically. Six presses, one word on the screen, six variants of one pad. Names now draw in the small font at nine characters and keep their trailing digits , so every press shows its move. Fifty-one starting points The rig ships with fifty-one more snapshots beside the factory one — 031 to 080 and 101 , all in bank 000 . Six each of house, deep house, minimal, dub and trance from 120 to 140 BPM, then twenty space presets, then 101 as an eleventh dub. All fifty-one were rebuilt on 4 September 2026, and it is worth knowing what changed, because the old ones were wrong in ways you would have blamed on yourself. Every preset had its eight faders at one identical setting, so nothing was mixed and whichever part was busiest won. Not one of them made a chord. Their drum grooves were fixed lists of steps with nothing behind them, so HITS and ROTATE showed numbers unrelated to what you heard and the first turn of either threw the groove away. Nineteen had a bass that played the flat seventh or the fifth on every sixteenth and never once the root. Now: a staged mix per family, sevenths in house and ninths in deep and a real triad in dub, euclidean grooves the panel agrees with, a bass of two to four notes a bar starting on the root, and swing on the hats. 061 – 080 are the space presets, and they are twenty rooms. Plate, chamber, hall, cathedral, tile, cavern, spring, gated, ambience, slapback, canyon, studio, basement, stairwell, glass, tunnel, chapel, hangar, closet, observatory. Three parts and eight modulators each, so there is nothing in the way of the room. They replaced twenty effect demos, eleven of which were note-for-note copies of another preset. Each family carries its own pair of effects, and the drone presets carry one each — nineteen pairs across the seventy-one. House goes into a small room, deep house into a hall, minimal into the driest plate, dub through a proper dub delay, and the twenty drones each have a different reverb rather than twenty settings of one. The space series keeps the factory reverb, because its twenty rooms are twenty values of the one control only that reverb has. They are fixed arrangements, not generative patches. Every voice arrives at LOCK — MELODY and RHYTHM both 0 — and nothing is modulated. Load one and it plays the same bar until you change something. That is deliberate: the rest of this instrument is about evolution, and these are the places to start from. Turn MELODY up and the preset becomes generative under your hands. The five drum channels keep their roles. A is always the kick and E always the open hat; what changes is the machine — TR909 for house, TR808 and CR78 for dub, TR606 for minimal, SP-1200 for lo-fi. Kits are mixed across channels the way they are on a record, so a 909 kick can sit under an 808 clap. 031 – 060 use the delay and reverb you already know. 061 – 080 replace that pair with something else on every chain — tape and chorus, vinyl and room, phaser and hall — a different pair on each, none repeated. On those twenty, the REVERB and DELAY encoders still send to whatever now occupies those two slots, so the labels stay put while the sound does not. 101-dub-mutated is the odd one out. Every other preset in the pack gives its three voices different synths; this one runs all three on the same engine and separates them by register, octave and gate instead — a bass on the one and the offbeat doubled at the octave, a triad stab strictly offbeat, a fifth held above it. 120 BPM, B-flat pentatonic, TR909 throughout. Load one from the touchscreen, inside bank 000 . Nothing is created or destroyed while you play, so a snapshot change is the one moment the audio graph is rebuilt. Twenty that never sit still Snapshots 081 – 100 are the opposite instrument. The fifty above hold still until you move something; these have almost no rhythm and seven or nine slow modulators each, and they hold continuously rather than restarting. These were the worst of the old presets and they are the most changed. All twenty used to be the same piece — identical registers, identical rhythms, twenty different reverbs over one arrangement. All eight channels attacked the first step together, and the chord that came out had no root in it, a minor second at the very bottom where the ear hears one rough beating tone rather than two notes, and two channels in exact unison doing no extra work. And they could not sustain: on a one-bar grid the longest note this instrument can hold is half a bar , so each “drone” played half a bar, stopped, and then all eight hit again — a chug, at two to four seconds a cycle. What you get now is five layers, none of which ever start at the same instant. Two run four bars long, two run two, and their notes butt against each other so the sound is continuous while the harmony moves underneath. Sixteen entries across a four-bar cycle and no two together, which is meant to make the bar line impossible to hear. The key walks slowly — every eight bars on a drone, every four on an ambient one — and because a key change moves every voice by the same amount, nothing that was in tune stops being in tune. 081 – 090 are drones, 091 – 100 ambient — the ambient ones add a soft brushed percussion channel. Tempos run 60 to 80. Two of them, 088 and 093 , are pentatonic and deliberately carry four layers instead of five: with five notes to the octave instead of seven a triad is half again as wide, and the fifth layer had nowhere to sit that was not already occupied. These use SHIFT + GRID, saved. A channel plays as a voice only because the snapshot carries that override, so on a drone you will see GRID blinking and the page indicator reading VOX on channels A, B and C, which are normally drums. That is the instrument telling you the channel is not itself — it is the state, not a fault. Press SHIFT + GRID on one to hear it as a drum again. Four of the ambient presets leave E on its sampler rather than giving it a synth, so the Turing register walks the kit's own samples. It is the trick the factory snapshot uses on the same channel, and it sounds nothing like a synth pad. The modulation is bar-synced and deliberately slow — the slowest rate is a full sixteen bars, which at 60 BPM is a sweep over a minute long. Nothing here needs your hands to stay interesting. Turn any modulated knob and you steer the centre of its sweep rather than fighting it. The synth engines this is proven on Twenty-four LV2 synths, plus the sampler. Every one below has been run on this rig at eight instances at once, which is the hardest thing this instrument does. Nothing here is a recommendation from a plugin list; it is what has actually played. Nine of them are not in a shipped snapshot any more , and that is a consequence of the 4 September rebuild rather than a verdict on them. The rebuilt presets choose an engine by its default polyphony — a chord collapses silently on a synth that comes up monophonic, or with two voices — and by whether it publishes a filter cutoff for the modulators to reach. That narrowed the set the packs use. The measurement stands either way , which is why they stay on this list: they load, they run eight-up, and any of them is a sound you can dial in yourself. Engine What kind of synth it is Where it plays padthv1 additive pad synth — PADsynth, huge slow spectra factory, both packs Obxd virtual analogue poly, Oberheim OB-X voicing factory, genre pack JC303 TB-303 emulation — mono acid bass, one filter, accent factory, genre pack Mutated Instruments macro-oscillator voice: one control picks the synthesis model, and it publishes more ports than anything else here both packs — it carries the chords in every genre preset and the drone ones Monique monophonic virtual analogue, aggressive filters genre pack — the bass amsynth two-oscillator analogue-modelled subtractive drone pack — the sub anchor String machine divide-down string ensemble — one sound, done well drone pack — the bass layer Helm subtractive poly built around heavy modulation drone pack — the upper voice Kars Karplus–Strong plucked string drone pack — the air layer Surge XT hybrid poly: wavetable, FM and subtractive in one voice drone pack Odin2 semi-modular unison drone pack RipplerX physically modelled resonators — strings, membranes, plates drone pack synthv1 four-oscillator subtractive poly measured, not currently shipped MDA JX10 two-oscillator
