second 303 — Nekobee, squarer than JC303 measured, not currently shipped Vex three-oscillator subtractive poly with its own arpeggiator measured, not currently shipped MiniOPL3 OPL3 chip emulation — two-operator FM, early-90s PC measured, not currently shipped LinuxSampler the SFZ sampler behind every drum channel and the kit walk everywhere Two engines will collapse a chord and neither says so. Obxd’s voice count is a control like any other and the factory snapshot ships it at two voices ; padthv1 has a mono switch, and the preset whose name makes it the obvious pad — Haze01 — has it on. Ask either for a triad and you get one note, at the right pitch, with nothing on the panel to explain the other two. If you are dialling in chords yourself, check the voice count first. One synth is out. SO-kl5 Piano Synthesizer was in a drone preset and cost 57.6 % of a core with 11 xruns at eight instances; it was replaced with RipplerX and that preset now runs at 38.6 % with none. It is the only engine on this rig that failed — a probe carrying six otherwise-unproven synths at once measured 16.4 %, so synths are not what runs this Pi out of headroom. Effects are; see Mixing and effects . Any other LV2 synth Zynthian can load will work with the surface — the four page-1 knobs rebind by name and the generated pages are built from whatever it publishes. Untested means untested, not unsupported. RANGE narrows the kit walk When a drum channel is played by the Turing register, RANGE decides how much of the kit it may reach. It is encoder 3 of that channel's CONTROL page, because how wide the walk is belongs to the sound rather than to the pattern. It arrives at 1, which is one note : the channel keeps playing its own drum and the register decides only which steps sound . That is the useful thing most of the time — you get rhythm you could not have programmed, on the drum you chose. Turn it up and the walk widens outward from that drum , taking in its neighbours in the kit, until at 4 it may use the whole thing. That is where a hats channel starts hitting kicks, which is occasionally what you want and usually not. On a synth channel RANGE means octave spread instead, and it sits on that channel's STEP page. The column follows the engine, as the sound page always has — a kit walk only exists where there is a kit. title: The surface

headings.text: One rule for every modifier: tap to keep it, hold to borrow it

body: The surface What every button does, how to read the two displays, and the list to work down when a channel goes quiet. This panel has one grammar and it is worth having before anything else. Four modes decide what the eight knobs mean. The channel decides what they act on. Holding ALL asks the same question of all eight channels at once. Every modifier obeys one rule about tapping and holding, every light means one of five things, and one press of the big encoder puts it all back. Learn those four sentences and the rest of this page is reference rather than reading. What you do with the panel — arming a drop, launching a scene, holding the machine still — is on Performing . Modes, pages and the lens Four buttons latch a mode , and exactly one is lit brightly at any time. The other three sit dim — they are still there, they are just not where you are. Button The question it answers The eight encoders become CONTROL How does this channel sound? the kit or preset, the filter, the sends STEP What does this channel play? hits, rotation, length, velocity, odds, swing — and on a voice, the chord AUTO What does the machine do to it by itself? which generator draws, how fast it changes, how far it may go, and how the phrase is built VOLUME What holds for everything? key, tempo, master, the shared reverb and delay AUTO is where the generator lives , which is what the button is printed for. RULE and MODEL choose which generator draws the part; MELODY and RHYTHM are how fast it changes its mind; LANE is how far out it may wander; MOVE is how often it may touch this channel at all; and PHRASE, FILL and EXIT are how the part is built and how it leaves. On a voice a second page, LINE , carries how the line of pitches is built — ROTATE, SPAN, STRIDE, FEED, AMT and RANGE. RANGE moved there when CHORD took its slot on STEP: it answers the same question the rest of that page asks, which is how far the line is spread. SPAN and STRIDE draw dead unless MODEL is on WALK, and that is the picture rather than a fault. The fifth button, ALL, is not a mode. It is the lens. Hold it and the eight encoders stop being eight verbs of one channel and become one verb across all eight channels — whichever knob your hand last moved. The page indicator says which: ALL CHANCE . Let go and you are back where you were, on the same page, with the same channel selected. That is the fast way to ask the question you actually ask mid-jam. You are setting the hats' odds, you wonder what the other seven are doing, you hold ALL with your other hand and there they are — eight columns, one per channel, and the knob under your finger still moves the same parameter. You never leave the channel you were looking at. A channel that does not carry the verb draws dead, exactly as it does anywhere else: hold ALL on CUTOFF and the three voices are live while the five drums show ---- , and hold it on LANE and it is the other way round. That is not a fault, it is the picture — it tells you which channels the question even applies to. Turning a global does not move the lens. There is only one BPM, one ROOT, one MASTER, so there is nothing to lay side by side; the same goes for a kit or a preset name, where eight lists share no index, and for a plugin's own ports, where the eight channels run three different synths and a matching name is not a matching control. Turn one of those and the lens keeps whatever it was last holding. With nothing moved yet it shows LEVEL. It follows the channel you select. Set the lens to something only a drum has, then select a voice, and it falls back to LEVEL rather than showing you a row of dead columns — a verb the selected channel cannot reach is a page with nothing on it, under a button you are holding down. The arrows beside the display choose the verb while the lens is open. They have no pages to walk there, so they walk the verbs instead — every one the selected channel carries, in panel order, wrapping at both ends. That is what makes “the knob your hand last moved” safe: it is exactly right for the knob you were just on and arbitrary for the one you want next, and the difference is now one arrow rather than leaving the lens, finding a page that carries the right verb, turning it and coming back. Tap ALL instead of holding it and it stays. That is the rule for every modifier on this panel — see below — and it is what you want when you are going to work across the eight for a while and need both hands. Pressing any mode button drops it , because a mode press means I am working somewhere else now . A mode can carry a second page. The arrows beside the display step through that mode's ring and wrap, and the big encoder does the same thing faster. Most rings are one page now, and the arrows go dark when there is nowhere to step — a lit arrow that cannot move is exactly the kind of lie this surface is built not to tell. Each mode remembers its own page separately for drum and voice channels. The big encoder has two exceptions, one silence and one press. While MOD is on it scales the depth of every live modulator at once rather than walking pages; while the bank grid is up it walks the four pages of banks. Inside the lens it does nothing at all — the arrows are stepping a verb there, not a page, and one control walking a list while a bigger one walks nothing is better than the big one yanking you off the verb your eight fingers are on. It has no light, so this page is the only place that can tell you. And pressing it is HOME . HOME is one press, from anywhere. It puts you back in the default performance state — STEP, page 1, every latch dropped, the pads showing what the selected channel is playing. Your channel stays selected, and nothing armed is cancelled : HOME is navigation, not a deletion. It is the button to hit when you have stopped knowing where you are, and it is the biggest, most central thing on the panel, which is deliberate — you have to be able to find it without looking. Pressing the mode you are already in returns you to page 1 of that mode. Every mode button means the same thing twice over: this mode, from the top . Group A–H selects the channel. Pads, tabs and all eight encoders follow immediately, and the inverted tab on the display — never a Group LED — is the authority on which channel is selected. One rule for every modifier: tap to keep it, hold to borrow it A tap latches. A hold is momentary. Every modifier on this panel obeys it, without exception: SHIFT, SELECT, DUPLICATE, MUTE, NAVIGATE, SWING, PAD MODE, SOLO and F1–F8. You hold what you are about to let go of, and you tap what should stay — and both routes reach the same state , so you never have to decide which you meant before you start. A second tap is always the way out. There is nothing on this surface you can enter with one gesture and need a different one to leave. Which one you are in is on the button. Held is steady , latched blinks . That distinction matters exactly once, and it is the moment it matters most: a latched modifier survives your finger leaving it, and an unlit one would be a mode you had walked away from without knowing. Two latched at once, and the one nearer the front wins the pads. Nothing stops you latching SHIFT and MUTE and MOD together, so there is a fixed order and it never changes: SHIFT, then ARM, then BANK, then MUTE, then MOD, then NAVIGATE . The winner owns the sixteen pads; the others keep doing everything they do off the pads — MOD still puts depth on the encoders, ARM still counts down on SELECT — and take the pads back the moment the one above them goes out. SHIFT is at the front because per–step odds is the one you reach for mid–bar with something else already latched. The single exception runs the other way: hold ARM while MOD is on and MOD keeps the pads , because that combination is RISE and it needs a shape pad, not a macro pad. The bar of the phrase appears on the indicator only when something is waiting to land. Arm a macro and the indicator counts 4/16 , 5/16 and so on, so a timed gesture has something to resolve against; with nothing pending the number is not drawn. That is deliberate and it is not only tidiness — a number that changes by itself made the instrument redraw both screens once a bar for as long as the music ran, which is the one kind of traffic this controller does not tolerate. The countdown is on the ARM lamp either way, and a light is free where a screen is not. A latched overlay also names itself on the display — STEP BANK , STEP MUTE , STEP ODDS . Six of them share the same sixteen pads, and the obvious answer of a colour each does not fit this hardware: the eight channel hues leave only two gaps wide enough to be told apart, and both are already spent. So the pads cannot say whose they are, and while you hold a modifier they do not need to — your hand knows. A latch is the one you can walk away from, and that is the one the indicator names. Reading the displays Both displays carry a tab row across the top — A–D on the left, E–H on the right — with four encoder columns under each. On a generated page the tab row carries parameter names instead — the names need the room. On CONTROL that page is the selected channel’s own plugin; on VOLUME it is the reverb, the delay or the master insert, one page each, reaching every remaining port of an effect that is ganged across all eight chains. See Deep parameter control . Everywhere else the tab row is the channels: A column drawn in lower case with ---- and no bar cannot act , and that is the instrument telling you so rather than failing quietly. A sampler publishes no filter, so CUTOFF draws dead on a drum; a chain with no kits loaded draws KIT dead, because there is nothing for the knob to step through. The encoder above a dead column does nothing, deliberately — the alternative is a knob that looks live and is not. The inverted tab is the selected channel. A dashed tab means that channel is not sounding , whether it is muted at the mixer or silenced by its own generator. It is the one mechanism this instrument has for explaining silence, so read the tab row before assuming a fault. A KICK B SNAR C CLAP D CHAT KIT SP12 SAMPLE 0003 RANGE 4 ctrl4 ---- A drum channel on CONTROL. KIT and SAMPLE are live; the three slots after them draw dead in lower case with ---- , because a sampler publishes no controller this surface could put there, and the encoder does nothing rather than pretending. RANGE is one of the dead three here — it is the kit–walk window, so it only comes alive on a channel whose kit actually walks. What the lights mean Every button on this panel except the eight Group buttons is a single colour. That leaves three brightnesses and two movements, and the whole surface uses only those five . Signal What it means, everywhere dark this button would do nothing right now — or the thing it shows is off dim available, and not acting bright acting — or your finger is on it blinking latched. You tapped it, your hand has left, and it is still on a pulse on the bar counting down to a boundary. Only SELECT does this, and only while a macro is armed Two things follow from that and both are worth knowing before you look at the panel. A light that is always on is not a light — so nothing here is lit just to show the instrument is running. And dark means the button is inert , not that it is missing: the display arrows go dark on a ring with one page, and the left STEP arrow is dark because nothing is bound to it yet. Surface What it says Group A–H hue is the channel, brightness is its level, dark means it is not sounding. A channel you have locked blinks — MOVE at LOCK is a standing decision, so it wears the same blink everything latched does, and you can see it from any page. While a modifier is held the row answers that modifier instead: ARM shows who survives a drop, and ERASE shows which channels hold a take you would lose — those go amber, the colour a played step wears everywhere here Mode buttons bright on the one you are in, dim on the other three. It cannot disagree with the display ALL the lens: dim, bright while held, blinking while latched F1–F8 bright while that channel is muted (or soloed, while the row means solo), dim while it is audible, dark where there is no channel at all PLAY bright while anything is running, dim while stopped — a stopped instrument is when you most need to find that button SOLO bright while held, blinking while solo mode is latched — that is, while F1–F8 are solos rather than mutes — and also blinking whenever anything is still soloed, even after you have left solo mode PAD MODE FREEZE. Blinking while the generators are held, bright while you hold it and the LFOs are parked too SHIFT, SELECT, DUPLICATE, MUTE, NAVIGATE, SWING the six modifiers, all the same: dim available, bright held, blinking latched PATTERN the regenerate button. Dim when a press would do something, dark when it would not — a reroll refuses on a channel you have played, and a refusal you cannot see is the same fault as a channel that goes silent without saying why SCENE dark. Nothing is bound to it REC dim when a take is possible, bright while you hold it — dark in STEP mode and while MOD is on. Red whenever an audio capture is being written , on any page: a file filling the disk outranks whether an overdub is possible here GRID dim — it does nothing on its own. Blinking while the selected channel is on an overridden kind, which is a latched state like any other NOTE REPEAT dim while the selected channel behaves as a voice, dark on a euclidean one where there is no register to give back TEMPO dim, bright while held. It does not latch STEP ▶ dim, bright while you hold the beat repeat RESTART dim — and bright while MOD is on , because there it is the pump SELECT the one exception, and it earns it: while a macro is armed this light is the countdown , one pulse per bar, steady through the bar it lands on. A modifier light and a countdown cannot both be on one LED, and the countdown is the one you need from across a room ERASE, the display arrows dim. ERASE goes bright while you hold it; an arrow goes dark when there is nothing for it to step — a one-page ring, and nowhere else, because in the lens it steps the verb The buttons, one by one NOTE REPEAT — the register undo. On a voice, it gives back the previous Turing line: it restores the earlier registers — both of them, so the rhythm cannot move out from under a line you just recovered — forces MELODY and RHYTHM to 0 so it holds, and rewrites immediately. It walks back up to four registers, which is roughly two wraps of human reaction time — the window in which a mutation steals a phrase before your hand arrives. It does nothing on a euclidean channel, which is why it is unlit there. DUPLICATE is the bank grid — sixteen whole arrangements on the pads. See below . The big encoder's press is HOME. STEP, page 1, every latch dropped, your channel and everything armed left alone. It is the one press that always means the same thing. TEMPO — hold it and every encoder turns twice as fast. The knobs are deliberately fine, so that a value can be crept up on rather than jumped over. TEMPO is how you cross a range in a hurry: hold it to get near, let go to land. It changes nothing but speed and it does not latch. It does not set the tempo either — that is BPM, encoder 3 of the VOLUME page, and it is on this panel like everything else. SHIFT + GRID switches the selected channel's kind — see Sound and presets . A bare GRID press does nothing, deliberately, and the button sits dim rather than lit to say so. MOD + ERASE + ALL clears every modulator at once, returning each value to the base you set — see Modulation . Three keys, two of them modifiers, because it is destructive and nothing destructive happens on this panel from a single press. PATTERN regenerates , and a press is enough — the reroll lands at the wrap, and a second press before then takes it back. The channel you have selected decides which half of the instrument it touches , so there is nothing to choose. ERASE and the same button undoes a reroll that already landed; SHIFT widens it to every channel of that channel's engine type. See Reroll . BROWSE, SAMPLING and ENTER do nothing either , and never have. They sit dark with the rest of the unbound panel. They are named here so that a dark button is never a question: on this surface dark means nothing would happen , and that is as true of a button with no job as of one whose job is unavailable right now. SCENE does nothing. It used to be the reroll button for the synths, back when the drums had their own; one button decides from the selected channel now, which is what a bare press always did anyway. The two buttons beside the big encoder step the selected channel's sound, and which sound depends on the engine: previous or next sample on a drum engine, previous or next preset on a synth engine. Hold SHIFT and they step the kit instead , on a drum engine only. Mute, solo and erase F1–F8 mute channels A–H , regardless of which channel is selected — F3 always mutes CLAP. Tap and it latches; hold past a quarter of a second and it is momentary, back on release. Same button, both gestures: momentary is how you play a gesture, latched is how you make a decision. The mute is on the mixer strip rather than the sequencer track , which is why it survives a snapshot, shows on the touchscreen mixer, and takes the channel's reverb and delay tail with it. There is no exception any more. CONTROL used to take the row for a plugin's switches, which needed SHIFT + Fn to get mute back and a third rule for what MOD did to it — three meanings on the eight buttons you hit without looking. A switch column's own encoder already steps that switch through its positions and draws the plugin's own word for each, so the button was a second route to the same thing, paid for with the row's only meaning. See Switches . SOLO works the same two ways, and the latched one changes what the F row is. Hold SOLO and tap an F button and that channel is soloed for as long as you hold — additive, so several at once. Tap SOLO and it latches: the whole F row stops being mutes and becomes solos until you tap it again. SOLO blinks while that latch is on — the panel's word for latched, here as everywhere — which is the one thing telling you what the eight buttons under your hand currently mean, and while the row means solo it lights the soloed channels rather than the muted ones. Leaving solo mode does not un-solo anything, and SOLO keeps blinking to say so. Tapping SOLO again gives the F row back to the mutes; it does not touch the mixer, because a solo you set on purpose is not something a change of view should throw away. So a channel can still be soloed with the row showing mutes — and in that state SOLO goes on blinking , which is the panel telling you a decision of yours is still standing. The Group buttons say it too: every non-soloed channel is dark. To clear it, tap SOLO to get the row back, un-press the soloed channel, and tap out again. ERASE + a Group button silences that channel — or, on a channel you have recorded onto, hands the pattern back to the generator. Both are taking something away, which is why they share the one modifier that means that. Hold ERASE before you press anything and the Group row tells you what is at stake. A channel holding a take you played goes amber and full ; every other channel drops to the floor, because there the gesture only silences and you can turn HITS or CHANCE straight back up. Handing a take back is the one thing on this instrument you cannot undo, and it used to be invisible — a take on a channel you were not looking at looked exactly like one that had none. Transport Play starts or stops all eight channels together. The decision is taken once and applied to all eight, so they cannot drift into opposite states. Restart jumps every playhead to step 0 without stopping — for pulling channels back onto the one after a length change has phased them apart. Press Play once after loading a snapshot: loop mode is re-asserted on every transport start, and a fresh load is the one moment it may need it. Where you come back to The instrument has one place it calls home, and it is where it starts: STEP, page 1, channel A, nothing latched, the F row are mutes. The pads show what the selected channel is playing with the playhead sweeping over them, which is the one picture that is always true. Press the big encoder and you are there. From any mode, any page, with any number of things latched. Your channel stays selected and anything you have armed keeps counting — HOME moves you, it does not undo you. Every latch is dropped, SOLO included , because every one of them can hide the step picture and the step picture is what this button is for. A finger still on a button is left alone: that hold ends when the finger does. And the first turn after HOME counts. Press it, then turn — the page moves on that first detent, not the second. Worth saying because it is the gesture you make when you have stopped knowing where you are, and a knob that eats your first move is exactly the wrong answer to that. That press does one more thing you will never notice until you would have. The big encoder reports an absolute position rather than a movement, and it wraps once per revolution, so a long spin can make the next click jump. HOME takes the reading it finds as the new zero, which means the fix for that is the same button as the fix for everything else. When it goes quiet Work down this list before suspecting the rig. Most of it is things you did. Check What it looks like Is the tab dashed? the channel is muted, or its generator is silent HITS on a drum 0 hits is a silent channel, not a broken one CHANCE at 0 on a drum, no steps left on a voice nothing fires Is something soloed? every non-soloed Group button goes dark MASTER on the VOLUME page the global level, easy to leave down Did a drop run? it mutes every channel you did not nominate; F1–F8 lift a mute by hand GATE at its floor on a voice a slow-attack patch never gets far enough to sound If the machine itself has stopped, the page indicator says so. Instead of the usual page name you will see GEN STOPPED and a count of seconds. That means generation has stopped moving — not that a channel is muted, and not that the pattern is empty. The pads keep playing while it says that : the instrument drops to what it can still do rather than going quietly dead, so you can carry on hitting drums while the generator is stuck. It clears itself the moment things move again. A voice that is locked is not silent — LOCK freezes the pattern, it does not mute it. If a whole channel is dead while its tab looks healthy, the fault is below the instrument: see Internals for how the chain is wired, and Manual installation for the checks that catch a stale MIDI route. When the surface goes dead Different fault, opposite symptom: the music keeps playing and the controller stops answering. Pads do nothing, no light changes, the screens are frozen or blank. Nothing is wrong with the instrument — the patterns are still running and still being written; it is the USB connection to the controller that has stopped carrying anything. Unplug the Maschine and plug it back in. That is the fix, and it is the only one that reliably works — the controller comes back within a couple of seconds and the whole surface repaints itself : pads, button lights, the two screens, all of it, back to exactly what it was showing. You do not have to touch a knob to wake it up, and you do not have to restart anything. Your patterns never stopped. Do not go looking for the cause on the touchscreen or in a menu first. If the sound is still there, it is the cable. See also Performing — the phrase clock, ARM and the macros, the mute and bank grids, FREEZE and beat repeat Generating patterns — what HITS, CHANCE, MELODY and RHYTHM actually do Playing and recording — the pad colours in full Modulation — what the ~ and the dashed bar mean

title: What could come next

headings.text: It needs two decks, and this has one
It needs a model this hardware cannot run
It needs a sensor that is not there
It was measured, and the hardware said no

body: What could come next Sixty-four ideas for this instrument, and none of them is promised . Eight left the list on 31 August 2026 by being built, played and written up, and nine more left it on 1 September — the watchdog, the phrase, the cellular automaton, per-step odds, the leaning generator, EXIT, banks as scenes, the modulator’s shape on the screen, and the screens’ brightness. They are on the Features page now. Twelve more were rewritten rather than removed , because something adjacent shipped and the entry had come to describe a world that no longer exists — each of those now says what exists and what is still missing, which is more useful than either keeping it whole or deleting it. This page was regrouped on 31 August 2026. It used to be organised by when an idea arrived and which project suggested it, and it carried rank numbers. Both are gone. Where an idea came from does not help you decide whether you want it, and two rounds of numbering had reached the point where six numbers each named two different features. Ideas are grouped by what they would change about playing the instrument , and each carries a name. The tables are also numbered 1 to 64, straight down the page , so that an idea can be pointed at in a sentence — “thirty-four” rather than “how sacred beat one is”. The number is a position on this page and nothing more: it is not a rank, not a queue, and not a promise, and it moves when an entry is built or removed. The name is the identity; the number is only a handle for today’s reading. What this page is Everything else in this guide describes an instrument you can play today. This page is the opposite: it is the idea list, kept in the open so that anyone forking the project can see what has been considered and how expensive it looked. The list was assembled by reading the code rather than by wishing — every entry has a known mechanism behind it, and several were rejected as impossible before they reached this page. Ideas that turned out to be already built have been removed rather than quietly left in, and everything that IS built is listed on the Features page, so that nobody has to guess whether something is a gap or a feature. What was considered and rejected is written down too, in Considered and refused — grouped by the reason, because the reason is the part that transfers to anyone forking this. Cost is S, M or L. S means a day or less and nothing new underneath. M means new state or a new part of the surface, still inside the shape the instrument already has. L means a new mechanism, a new page of the surface, or a question that cannot be answered without measuring the hardware first. Impact is 1 to 5, and it means musical consequence — how much the thing you hear changes — not how clever the idea is. Within each section the strongest ratio of impact to cost comes first. That ratio is where an argument starts, not where it ends: it knows nothing about what depends on what. The countdown ruler ranked twenty-second while nine of the entries above it could not exist without it, which is why it was the first thing built. Ideas this instrument already has Most lists of generative and DJ tools suggest the same things, and a good part of that list is already built here. That catalogue moved to its own page on 1 September 2026: it had grown past the point where it belonged inside an idea list, and a reader arriving with “does it do X?” should not have to read a page about what does not exist yet to find out that it does. → Features — every feature, in one list, each linked to the page that walks you through it. Read the two together. This page is what is missing ; that one is what is there ; and the section at the end of this page is what will not be built at all, with the reason. The instrument plays itself The instrument can invent a bar and it can schedule a gesture. Between those two there is nothing that decides what the next eight bars should be. This is the section that would fill that gap — and the safety it needs, because a machine that arranges by itself must also be able to say when it has stopped. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 1 An arranger that mutes and unmutes Exactly one part enters or leaves every eight bars, chosen by the machine — adding while the track is thin, stripping while it is crowded, and never bringing in a channel with nothing in it. The whole arrangement is which channels are silent, and the tension comes entirely from what is missing. S 5 2 One cue, answered by every part Every eight bars the machine draws a single instruction, and the bass, the hats, the percussion and the chords each answer that same instruction in their own idiom. Today the channels wander independently, which never sounds like a decision. M 5 3 Auto-pilot Arm a build and a drop to repeat on a sixteen or thirty-two bar cycle, and the instrument plays its own arrangement while you work on a sound. S 4 4 The same bar tomorrow Variation worked out from the seed and the bar number rather than from whatever has happened since. Half of this is already true and it is the half nobody expected : a voice’s line is a pure function of one saved integer, so the register does come back exactly. What does not exist is the bar number part — the counter is advanced by rewrites rather than derived from where you are, so nothing can be computed ahead, and the drums have no equivalent at all. S 4 5 Generate three, keep the best Compose a few candidate bars, score them, and play the best one. A cheap generator and a cheap judge beat an expensive generator, and the judge is the same one the constraint knob would use. M 4 6 A style as odds rather than a fixed snapshot The snapshot packs are frozen settings. This is the same pack expressed as distributions and hard rules, so a style becomes a region to wander inside rather than a single point. It ships, offline. tools/style-sampler.py samples and blends, including the rule that settings which cannot be averaged are taken whole from one parent — see Generating starting points of your own . What is left is the instrument: nothing in the driver can read a distribution, so a style is still a fixed point once it is on the rig. L 4 7 A seed you can see and save The premise here was wrong and it is worth saying so. A voice’s randomness is not gone forever once it moves — the register is one integer, it is saved, and it comes back exactly. What is missing is only the seeing : no page carries a seed, so a line you liked is recoverable by loading the snapshot and not by writing a number down. S 3 8 Rules checked and repaired at every write A named list of things that must be true of each kind of part — four-to-the-floor stays on the quarters, the bass stays off the one, open hats keep their distance — checked and corrected as the pattern is written instead of hoped for. S 3 9 The night review The instrument has written a structured line for every event since it was built, and nothing has ever read one back. A summary of a jam — what drifted, what was rerolled, which channels were muted longest, how far the tempo moved — is a tool over a file that already exists. S 3 Building, landing, breaking Gestures you fire that resolve somewhere musical, four or eight or sixteen bars later, instead of happening the instant your finger moves. That rested on something the instrument did not have — a sense of which bar it was on. It has one now : the phrase clock and ARM , DROP , the CHANCE ramp and RISE are built and written up. What is below is what else could fire into that clock. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 10 The build ladder One number from 0 to 100 that moves hits, density, odds, ratchet and cutoff together. Turn it by hand, or arm it and let it climb over sixteen bars. M 5 11 Tempo ramp Six BPM over eight bars into the drop, then hold or snap back. S 4 12 One-shot fills A second pattern per channel, fired by a pad, played once, returning to the loop by itself. FILL is not this , though it is close enough to be worth separating: FILL adds density to the last bar of a phrase and returns on its own, but it is a knob rather than a pad, and it decorates the same line rather than swapping in another one. S 4 13 TURN The bar before any landing becomes a fill, and the original pattern comes straight back. Every build ends on a turnaround. M 4 14 BRAKE Hold a button and the tempo bends down; release and it returns at the next bar. A tape-stop that resolves. M 4 15 Timed transpose Up a fifth for eight bars, and back, with the return already paid for. M 4 16 Sampled risers and impacts A sample scheduled backwards from the boundary so its tail lands on the drop. The player for it is already running and idle. Not the shipped riser, which is a one-shot modulator sweep and carries no audio. M 4 17 Velocity swell The pattern leans harder across a build and settles after the drop. S 3 18 Silence before the drop The bar before a landing goes quiet on the parts you nominate, and everything else plays straight through, so the drop hits harder. BREAK at length 1 already makes this sound ; what it does not do is the arrangement half — it fires under your finger instead of being anchored to a landing, and it mutes mixer strips rather than nominating parts. S 3 19 Retrograde The bar plays backwards for N bars and then unmirrors. M 3 20 Count-in Once a drop is armed, the last bar clicks, so you can play into it instead of counting. S 2 21 Loop roll Hold a button and the channel loops the last eight, four, two or one steps around the playhead, then rejoins. The beat repeat on STEP ▶ is the neighbouring answer : a fixed one beat, from the pattern’s start, on every generated channel at once. It sidesteps the timing question rather than answering it — a selectable window around where the playhead actually is is still the hard part, and still not built. L 5 22 Note repeat Hold a pad and it retriggers at a chosen rate — the Maschine gesture this instrument does not have. Measured, and mostly refused : the driver’s heartbeat leaves a quarter-note repeat about seven per cent out and a sixteenth about twenty-eight, so only the slowest rate could be offered honestly, and that is not what a player means by note repeat. Left here as an open question rather than a plan. L 2 How a pattern is made The generator owns the pattern, and everything here changes what it is allowed to write — either by giving it a new way to invent, or by giving you a way to overrule it that survives the next bar. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 23 How much the machine may move a channel One number per channel, from nothing to everything. At zero the channel holds its pattern rigidly bar to bar, so the tops can move while the kick stays put. MOVE ships — see MOVE — and most of the caveat below has been closed since this entry was written: the ratchet, chance and timescale ticks, the gate collapse, FILL and the beat repeat all ask now. The drop still does not. The chord walker now holds when every voice is locked, which is as far as it can honestly go: it moves ROOT, and ROOT is one setting shared by all three voices, so it cannot be gated for one of them without giving each voice a key of its own. Lock one voice while its neighbours are open and the key still moves under it. What follows is the original entry. The generators themselves already ask before they write; what does not ask is the bar-rate gestures — the ratchet, chance and timescale ticks, the drop, and the chord walker moving the key — each of which walks every channel whether or not you had an opinion about that one. S 5 24 A hole the generator may not fill This makes a step the machine is not allowed to fill back in — the difference between what the generator owns and what you own, at the level of a single step. The old premise is gone : a tap no longer wipes on the next turn of a knob, because it lives in a register that survives ROTATE and drift. But it is not protected either — HITS, DIVIDE and LENGTH reset it by design, and RHYTHM’s own evolution can fill it back in. S 4 25 Bar conditions A step that plays only on the third bar of four, or the last of eight. The instrument already counts bars, so the pattern stops repeating without anything moving. S 4 26 Stay out of the kick’s way A channel that quietly drops any hit landing on the kick, so two parts cannot fight for the same instant. Beat one may still double it, because that is the one place they should agree. M 4 27 Reverse it every fourth bar Transforms that apply to a whole channel on a period: play backwards every fourth bar, rotate a step every third, thin out one hit in five. Every control this instrument has is a value; these would be the first that are rules. M 4 28 How far the generators may stray One knob for how narrow the danceable lane is. At the top, a bar is measured before it is allowed out and the weakest hits are removed until it holds together; at the bottom you get the raw field. LANE ships on the drums — see LANE . On the three voices the knob is there and the arm returns without acting, so what is left is a voice’s answer to “does this bar hold together”, which is not the same question. M 3 29 How sacred beat one is One number: at the top, the first step of a pulse channel always survives drift, rerolls and the random register; below it, the floor is allowed to drop out. It removes the one thing the generative side can do that a dancer notices immediately. S 3 30 Set a step’s pitch with two taps Hold SHIFT, tap the step, tap the pad whose note you want. One grid, two meanings, no menu. S 3 31 Accent and micro-timing A velocity accent mask and a small timing nudge per channel: the weight that swing alone does not give. M 3 32 A part derived from two others A hat that is defined as “wherever the kick and the clap disagree”. It cannot collide with either, because it is made of them. M 3 33 Euclid inside euclid Split a hat pattern with a second euclidean figure, so the closed and open hats divide a line neither could make alone. M 3 34 An undo ring for the rest Reroll has a one-deep undo and a voice’s register has a four-deep one; LENGTH and the pattern knobs have none. This would give them the same ring. M 3 35 Echo as real repeats Every hit spawning actual repeats rather than an effect, each repeat able to move in pitch — pitch inside the feedback loop. Musically one of the strongest ideas on this page and the worst fit for how this instrument works, because writing repeats into a pattern is a pattern rewrite, and that is banned for a reason. Recorded rather than planned. L 3 Voices, sound and the mix # Idea What it does Cost Impact 36 Mixer scenes A whole mixer picture — levels, pans, mutes — recalled at the next bar. Two or three make verse, chorus and drop. M 4 37 Spare chains A channel becomes a real synth rather than borrowing one, with somewhere to put it. L 4 38 A different drum engine Replacing the sampler with one that has a filter per drum — the only route to per-channel drum timbre that measurement has left open. L 4 39 Sound changes land on the bar A kit or preset change waits for the downbeat instead of arriving mid-beat, so sweeping through sounds stops leaving a seam. S 3 40 Trim that follows density Doubling a channel’s hits doubles its presence in the mix, and today you fix that by hand. This estimates how loud a part will be from the pattern as it is written, and trims it before you hear the problem. M 3 41 Duplicate a channel Copy a channel onto another group, pattern and settings and modulation, then let it diverge. M 3 42 A character insert A second effect slot per channel, for drive and colour rather than space. M 3 43 A different lead synth Surge XT on the factory snapshot’s LEAD chain, with its own parameter tables. It already ships on other chains in both snapshot packs; this is about the factory default. M 3 44 Tempo wander A fraction of a beat per minute of slow drift, to take off the last of the machine-grid feel. Small, and worth knowing that it deliberately gives up an exactness the factory snapshot was tuned for. S 2 45 Choke groups Closed hat kills open hat. Measured, and the sampler will not do it : a one-shot plays its sample to the end whether or not a note-off arrives. Any version of this has to cut the sound somewhere else. L 2 What the panel shows Two screens of one-bit glass, sixteen pads and a ring of encoders. This instrument has one law it cannot break — a silent channel must say why — and most of this section is that law applied to things the machine now decides on its own. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 46 A view that stops computing what it hides A display mode that does not merely hide the busy parts of the screen but stops working them out at all. On a rig whose one hard failure is a saturated connection to the controller, a view that removes work rather than pixels is a safety feature rather than a preference. S 3 47 Curves and waveforms on the screens The screens draw text, bars and now a modulator’s wave silhouette . The dirty-rectangle work this entry was waiting on has landed , so a patch of screen is affordable. What is left is the drawing itself: there is no line or per-pixel primitive, only whole glyphs and filled blocks. “A wave that moves” stays banned whatever the primitives allow — animating a value on these screens is the one thing measured to throw this controller off the bus. L 3 48 A groove report Every bar, a few numbers for what the pattern actually turned out to be: how syncopated, how dense, how much of it lands on the beat. It is the natural readout for the constraint knob and the weighted generator, which otherwise change a pattern with nothing on the surface explaining why. The question was whether a gesture that only ever removes still has a meaning now that a bare tap both adds and removes. It does, and the meaning is ownership: on a pattern you recorded the notes are the truth and removing them is the erase, which is what it always did; on a pattern the machine writes, the register is the truth, so it clears the step there instead and the step stays gone. The original entry follows. A bare pad tap now both adds and removes a step, so ERASE + pad may have no job left. Worse, the two write to different places: ERASE deletes the note straight out of the pattern while a tap writes the register, so an erased step quietly returns at the next rewrite. The screen is drawn in three bands now — the tabs, the page indicator and each of the four encoder columns — and each one erases only its own box and is sent only when its own contents changed. Turning one encoder costs about a seventh of what a repaint cost before , and selecting a channel about a fifth; a repaint where genuinely everything moved is slightly cheaper than the old one rather than worse. The original entry follows. Every repaint clears the framebuffer first, which forces a full-screen transfer: 2120 bytes per changed display where a single changed column would need about 300. It is the one path that has thrown the controller off the USB bus, and it is what makes “never animate a value on the screens” a rule rather than a preference. L 2 Considered and refused The ideas above survived a filter. This is what did not, grouped by the reason rather than by where it came from — because the reason is the part that transfers. If you are forking this instrument and one of these looks tempting, the paragraph under it is the argument you would have to beat. It needs two decks, and this has one Automatic transitions, crossfades, blends, isolator swaps, double drops, bridges, rewinds, beat-matching, tempo alignment between tracks, harmonic mixing by key wheel. A whole research literature exists here and almost none of it applies: this instrument has one deck and no tracks . There is nothing to transition from, and nothing to transition to. It generates the music rather than replaying it. One idea did survive the crossing, and it is on the list above: a part that closes through a filter rather than being switched off. That is what a good transition actually is, applied to a single channel instead of a whole track. It needs a model this hardware cannot run Real-time generative audio models, latent-space blending between sources, anything that infers a waveform. The Pi already runs eight audio chains and a sequencer with a hard real-time deadline; there is nothing left for inference. And the interaction those systems are built around is typing a description of the music you want, on an instrument that runs headless and has no keyboard . One thing did survive: their interface . Blending several weighted targets continuously, rather than fading from one preset to another, is a good idea independent of what does the generating — and it is on the list above as a pad gesture. It needs typing Live-coding environments are the most powerful generative tools that exist, and none of them can be adopted here for the same dull reason: this is a control surface with sixteen pads, nine encoders and two small screens, and the rig has no monitor attached. What can be taken from them is the algebra rather than the language — transforms that apply to a whole channel on a period, which is on the list above. It needs a sensor that is not there Systems that read a crowd, or react to what is happening in a game, are answering a question this instrument cannot ask. There is no audience input and no game. The nearest real signal would be a MIDI controller plugged into the back, which is a mapping decision rather than a feature. It was measured, and the hardware said no Cutting one drum off with another. Closed hat killing open hat is standard on drum machines. The sampler here plays a one-shot to the end whether or not a note-off arrives — measured. Any version of this has to cut the sound somewhere else, which is why it stays on the list above at low value rather than being quietly dropped. Note repeat at useful rates. The driver's heartbeat leaves a quarter-note repeat about seven per cent out and a sixteenth about twenty-eight. Only the slowest rate could be offered honestly, and that is not what a player means by note repeat. A precise analogue master clock. The expansion bus this Pi has jitters by about a millisecond from user space — fine for pitch, and about eight tenths of a per cent of a sixteenth note at 125 BPM, which is wrong for anything trying to stay in time with it. Pitch and gates out are still worth doing and are on the list; the clock belongs on a MIDI socket instead. And the honest arithmetic Three surveys were run: thirty-one other projects built for this same controller, and about thirty-five generative and DJ music tools. The controller survey found not one generative technique in the entire set — no probability, no evolving state, no humanisation. The music-tool survey yielded five ideas that were new to this list. That is not a complaint about other people's work, which is frequently better than this at the things it set out to do. It is a note for whoever reads this next: the search is closer to saturated than it looks , and the remaining value is in building what is already on the list rather than in finding more of it. What the list says Read down the ratios and one shape appears: the cheapest strong ideas are all about restraint rather than invention. A number for how much the machine may move a channel, a step it is not allowed to fill, a rule that beat one survives, a part that closes instead of vanishing — four small pieces of work, and between them they answer the one complaint a generative instrument earns, which is that it will not leave anything alone. Two of those four have since been built , which is the best evidence the shape was real: MOVE and EXIT both shipped on 1 September, and both were cheap exactly as predicted. The expensive entries are expensive for the same reason, and it is not the code. Each needs a new page of the surface or a new answer about timing. On an instrument with sixteen pads and two small screens, where to put a thing is usually harder than how to build it. And several entries are honest unknowns, kept here rather than quietly dropped. Whether a sampled drum can be cut off at all, whether the driver’s heartbeat is fast enough to roll a single step, and whether the screens will accept a small rectangle instead of a full-width strip are all questions for the hardware. The third has been answered since — yes, and it is in use , which halved what a display update costs. The other two are still open. This project has learned twice that a feature written from the code rather than from the rig is a feature that gets published wrong.
